During the Second World War, the city and surrounding area were a target for air raids as heavy industry was involved in the production of ships and armaments. The raids caused 141 deaths and 587 injuries.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-63) A former French consul in Newcastle, Jacques Serre, assisted the German war effort by describing important targets in the region to [Admiral Raeder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erich_Raeder "Erich Raeder") who was the head of the German Navy.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-64)

The public sector in Newcastle began to expand in the 1960s. The federal structure of the [University of Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Durham "University of Durham") was dissolved. That university's college in Newcastle, which had been known as King's College, became the University of Newcastle upon Tyne (now known as [Newcastle University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University "Newcastle University")), which was founded in 1963,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-65) followed by Newcastle Polytechnic in 1969; the latter received university status in 1992 and became the University of Northumbria at Newcastle (now known as [Northumbria University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumbria_University "Northumbria University")).[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-66)

Further efforts to preserve the city's historic past continued in the later 20th century, with the opening of Newcastle Military Vehicle Museum in 1983 and [Stephenson Railway Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside_Steam_Railway "North Tyneside Steam Railway") in 1986. The Military Vehicle museum closed in 2006.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-67) New developments at the turn of the 21st century included the [Life Science Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Life "Centre for Life") in 2000 and [Millennium Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateshead_Millennium_Bridge "Gateshead Millennium Bridge") in 2001.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-68)

Based at [St James' Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James'_Park "St James' Park") since 1886, [Newcastle United F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_United_F.C. "Newcastle United F.C.") became [Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League "Football League") members in 1893.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-69) They have won four top division titles (the first in 1905 and the most recent in 1927), six [FA Cups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Cup "FA Cup") (the first in 1910 and the most recent in 1955), the [Inter-Cities Fairs Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-Cities_Fairs_Cup "Inter-Cities Fairs Cup") in 1969 and most recently the [League Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EFL_Cup "EFL Cup") in 2025, their first domestic trophy since 1955.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-70) They broke the world transfer record in 1996 by paying £15 million for [Blackburn Rovers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackburn_Rovers_F.C. "Blackburn Rovers F.C.") and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_national_football_team "England national football team") striker [Alan Shearer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Shearer "Alan Shearer"), one of the most prolific goalscorers of that era.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-71)

In 2017, Newcastle was the venue for the 2017 Freedom City festival. The 2017 Freedom City festival commemorated the 50 years since [Martin Luther King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr.")'s visit to Newcastle, where King received his honorary degree from [Newcastle University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University "Newcastle University").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-freedomCity2017_1-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-honDegreeKing-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-freedomCity-74) In 2018, Newcastle hosted [the Great Exhibition of the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Exhibition_of_the_North "The Great Exhibition of the North"), the largest event in England in 2018. The exhibition began on 22 June with an opening ceremony on the River Tyne, and ended on 9 September with the [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run") weekend. The exhibition describes the story of the north of England through its innovators, artists, designers and businesses.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-riverCeremonyOpeninExh2018-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-exOfNorth2018-76)

In 2019, a travel site named Newcastle to be the friendliest city in the UK.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-chroniclelive-77)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Side_-_Tyne_Bridge.jpg/250px-Side_-_Tyne_Bridge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Side_-_Tyne_Bridge.jpg)

Side, a street in Newcastle near the Tyne Bridge

Since 1974, Newcastle has been a part of the [metropolitan county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_county "Metropolitan county") of [Tyne and Wear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_and_Wear "Tyne and Wear") in [North East England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England "North East England"). The city is located on the north-western bank of the [River Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne "River Tyne"), approximately 46 miles (74 km) south of the border with Scotland.

The ground beneath the city is formed from [Carboniferous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carboniferous "Carboniferous")[strata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratum "Stratum") of the Middle Pennine Coal Measures Group — a suite of [sandstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone"), [mudstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudstone "Mudstone") and [coal seams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_seam "Coal seam") which generally dip moderately eastwards. To the west of the city are the Upper Pennine Coal Measures and further west again the sandstones and mudstones of the Stainmore Formation, the local equivalent of the [Millstone Grit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millstone_Grit "Millstone Grit").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-78)

In large parts, Newcastle still retains a [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval "Medieval") street layout. Narrow alleys or '[chares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chare "Chare")', most of which can only be traversed by foot, still exist in abundance, particularly around the [riverside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quayside "Quayside"). Stairs from the riverside to higher parts of the city centre and the extant [Castle Keep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_Castle_Keep "Newcastle Castle Keep"), originally recorded in the 14th century, remain intact in places. Close, Sandhill and [Quayside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quayside "Quayside") contain modern buildings as well as structures dating from the 15th–18th centuries, including [Bessie Surtees House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Surtees_House "Bessie Surtees House"), the Cooperage and Lloyds Quayside Bars, Derwentwater House and House of Tides, a restaurant situated at a Grade I-listed 16th century merchant's house at 28–30 Close.

The city has an extensive [neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") centre referred to as Tyneside Classical,[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Tyneside_Classical-79) largely developed in the 1830s by [Richard Grainger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Grainger "Richard Grainger") and [John Dobson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dobson_(architect) "John Dobson (architect)"). More recently, Newcastle architecture considered to be Tyneside classical has been extensively restored. Broadcaster and writer [Stuart Maconie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Maconie "Stuart Maconie") described Newcastle as England's best-looking city[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-81) and the German-born British scholar of architecture, [Nikolaus Pevsner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolaus_Pevsner "Nikolaus Pevsner"),[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Pevsner2010-07-26-82) describes [Grey Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey_Street,_Newcastle "Grey Street, Newcastle") as one of the finest streets in England. In 1948, the poet [John Betjeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Betjeman "John Betjeman") said of Grey Street, "As for the curve of Grey Street, I shall never forget seeing it to perfection, traffic-less on a misty Sunday morning."[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-greyStBetjeman-83) The street curves down from [Grey's Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey's_Monument "Grey's Monument") towards the valley of the [River Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne,_England "River Tyne, England") and was voted England's finest street in 2005 in a survey of [BBC Radio 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_4 "BBC Radio 4") listeners.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-85) In the Google Street View awards of 2010, Grey Street came 3rd in the British picturesque category.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-google_street_view-86) A portion of [Grainger Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grainger_Town "Grainger Town") was demolished in the 1960s to make way for the [Eldon Square Shopping Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldon_Square_Shopping_Centre "Eldon Square Shopping Centre"), including all but one side of the original [Eldon Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Eldon_Square "Old Eldon Square") itself.

Immediately to the north-west of the city centre is [Leazes Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leazes_Park "Leazes Park"), first opened to the public in 1873[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-87) after a petition by 3,000 working men of the city for "ready access to some open ground for the purpose of health and recreation". Just outside one corner of this is [St James' Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James'_Park "St James' Park"), the stadium home of [Newcastle United FC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_United_FC "Newcastle United FC") which dominates the view of the city from all directions.

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/St_James_Park_Newcastle_as_seen_from_south_of_the_River_Tyne.jpg/500px-St_James_Park_Newcastle_as_seen_from_south_of_the_River_Tyne.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_James_Park_Newcastle_as_seen_from_south_of_the_River_Tyne.jpg)

View of [St James' Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James'_Park "St James' Park") on the skyline and surrounding buildings, as seen from Gateshead

Another major [green space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_belt "Green belt") in the city is the [Town Moor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_Moor,_Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Town Moor, Newcastle upon Tyne"), lying immediately north of the city centre. It is larger than London's [Hyde Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park,_London "Hyde Park, London") and [Hampstead Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampstead_Heath "Hampstead Heath") put together[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-townmoo1-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-townmoo2-89) and the [freemen of the city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_City "Freedom of the City") have the right to graze cattle on it.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-townmoo1-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-townmoo2-89) The right extends to the pitch of [St. James' Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._James'_Park "St. James' Park"), [Newcastle United Football Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_United "Newcastle United")'s ground; this is not exercised, although the Freemen do collect rent for the loss of privilege. Honorary freemen include [Bob Geldof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Geldof "Bob Geldof"),[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-BobGeldof2010-09-17-90)[King Harald V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Harald_V "King Harald V") of Norway,[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-KingHNorway-91)[Bobby Robson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Robson "Bobby Robson"),[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-SirBobby2010-09-17-92)[Alan Shearer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Shearer "Alan Shearer"),[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-AlanShearer2010-09-17-93) the late [Nelson Mandela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela")[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Mandela2010-09-17-94) and the [Royal Shakespeare Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Shakespeare_Company "Royal Shakespeare Company").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-RoyalShakespeare-95)[The Hoppings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hoppings "The Hoppings") funfair, said to be the largest [travelling funfair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travelling_funfair "Travelling funfair") in Europe, is held here annually in June.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Hop2010-09-17-96)

In the south-eastern corner of the Town Moor is [Exhibition Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exhibition_Park,_Newcastle "Exhibition Park, Newcastle"), which contains the only remaining pavilion from the [North East Coast Exhibition of 1929](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Coast_Exhibition "North East Coast Exhibition"). From the 1970s until 2006, this housed the Newcastle Military Vehicle Museum; which closed in 2006. The pavilion is now being used as a [microbrewery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microbrewery "Microbrewery") and concert venue for [Wylam Brewery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wylam_Brewery "Wylam Brewery").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-97)

### Ouseburn

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Ouseburn")]

The wooded gorge of the [Ouseburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouseburn "Ouseburn") in the east of the city is known as [Jesmond Dene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesmond_Dene "Jesmond Dene") and forms another recreation area, linked by Armstrong Park and Heaton Park to the [Ouseburn Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouseburn_Valley "Ouseburn Valley"), where the river finally reaches the [River Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne,_England "River Tyne, England").

The springtime [dawn chorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn_chorus_(birds) "Dawn chorus (birds)") at 55 degrees latitude has been described as one of the best in the world.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-dawnChorus-98) The dawn chorus of the Jesmond Dene green space has been professionally recorded and has been used in various workplace and hospital rehabilitation facilities.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-dawnChorus-98)

### Quayside

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Quayside")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Quayside%2C_Newcastle_upon_Tyne.jpg/250px-Quayside%2C_Newcastle_upon_Tyne.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Quayside,_Newcastle_upon_Tyne.jpg)

Quayside architecture, showing the historic [Newcastle Guildhall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guildhall,_Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Guildhall, Newcastle upon Tyne") with its white turret

The area around the [Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne "River Tyne") Gorge, between Newcastle on the north bank and [Gateshead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateshead "Gateshead") on the south bank, is the famous Newcastle-Gateshead [Quayside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quayside "Quayside"). It is famed for its series of dramatic bridges, including the [Tyne Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_Bridge "Tyne Bridge") of 1928 which was built by [Dorman Long](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorman_Long "Dorman Long") of [Middlesbrough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesbrough "Middlesbrough"), [Robert Stephenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Stephenson "Robert Stephenson")'s [High Level Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Level_Bridge,_River_Tyne "High Level Bridge, River Tyne") of 1849, the first road/rail bridge in the world, and the [Swing Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_Bridge,_River_Tyne "Swing Bridge, River Tyne") of 1876.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-99)

Large-scale [regeneration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_renewal "Urban renewal") efforts have led to the replacement of former shipping premises with new office developments; a tilting bridge - the [Gateshead Millennium Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateshead_Millennium_Bridge "Gateshead Millennium Bridge") - integrated the Quayside more closely with the Gateshead Quayside, home to the [BALTIC Centre for Contemporary Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BALTIC_Centre_for_Contemporary_Art "BALTIC Centre for Contemporary Art") (the venue for the [Turner Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turner_Prize "Turner Prize") 2011)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-TurnerPrize2010-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-101) and the [Norman Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Foster,_Baron_Foster_of_Thames_Bank "Norman Foster, Baron Foster of Thames Bank")-designed [Glasshouse International Centre for Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasshouse_International_Centre_for_Music "Glasshouse International Centre for Music"). The Newcastle and Gateshead Quaysides are now a cosmopolitan area with bars, restaurants, hotels and public spaces.

### Grainger Town

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Grainger Town")]

Main article: [Grainger Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grainger_Town "Grainger Town")

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b1/Newcastle_England%2C_Grainger_Street_c._1906.jpg/250px-Newcastle_England%2C_Grainger_Street_c._1906.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Newcastle_England,_Grainger_Street_c._1906.jpg)

Grainger Street, circa 1906

The historic heart of Newcastle is the Grainger Town area. Established on classical streets built by [Richard Grainger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Grainger "Richard Grainger"), a builder and developer, between 1835 and 1842, some of Newcastle upon Tyne's finest buildings and streets lie within this area of the city centre including [Grainger Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grainger_Market "Grainger Market"), [Theatre Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_Royal,_Newcastle "Theatre Royal, Newcastle"), [Grey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_grey "Earl grey") Street, Grainger Street and [Clayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Clayton_(town_clerk) "John Clayton (town clerk)") Street.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) These buildings are predominantly four stories high, with vertical dormers, domes, turrets and spikes. Richard Grainger was said to 'have found Newcastle of bricks and timber and left it in stone'.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) Of Grainger Town's 450 buildings, 244 are [listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"), of which 29 are grade I and 49 are grade II*.

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Earl_Grey_atop_his_monument_%28geograph_2368405%29.jpg/250px-Earl_Grey_atop_his_monument_%28geograph_2368405%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Earl_Grey_atop_his_monument_(geograph_2368405).jpg)

Grey's Monument

[Grey's Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey's_Monument "Grey's Monument"), which commemorates Prime Minister [Earl Grey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Grey,_2nd_Earl_Grey "Charles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey") and his [Reform Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Act_1832 "Reform Act 1832") of 1832, stands above [Monument Metro station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_metro_station "Monument metro station") and was designed and built by [Edward Hodges Baily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Hodges_Baily "Edward Hodges Baily") and [Benjamin Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_and_Benjamin_Green "John and Benjamin Green"). Hodges, who also built [Nelson's Column](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson's_Column "Nelson's Column"), designed and built the statue,[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Baily2010-2010-07-26-104) and the monument plinth was designed and built by Benjamin Green.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-BenjaminGreen2010-07-26-105)

The Grainger Market replaced an earlier market originally built in 1808 called the Butcher Market.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Grain201308-106) The Grainger Market was Newcastle's first indoor market.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) At the time of its opening in 1835, it was said to be one of the largest and most beautiful markets in Europe.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) The opening was celebrated with a grand dinner attended by 2000 guests, and the Laing Art Gallery has a painting of this event.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) With the exception of the timber roof which was destroyed by a fire in 1901 and replaced by latticed-steel arches the Market is largely in its original condition.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) The Grainger Market architecture, like most in Grainger Town, which are either grade I or II listed, was listed grade I in 1954 by English Heritage.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Grain201308-106)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-107)

The development of the city in the 1960s saw the demolition of part of [Grainger Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grainger_Town "Grainger Town") as a prelude to the modernist rebuilding initiatives of [T. Dan Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._Dan_Smith "T. Dan Smith"), the leader of [Newcastle City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_City_Council "Newcastle City Council"). A corruption scandal was uncovered involving Smith and [John Poulson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Poulson "John Poulson"), a [property developer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate_developer "Real estate developer") from [Pontefract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontefract "Pontefract"), West Yorkshire, and both were imprisoned. Echoes of the scandal were revisited in the late 1990s in the [BBC TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_TV "BBC TV") series, _[Our Friends in the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Our\_Friends\_in\_the\_North "Our Friends in the North")_.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-108)

### Housing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Housing")]

The [Tyneside flat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyneside_flat "Tyneside flat") was the dominant housing form constructed at the time when the industrial centres on Tyneside were growing most rapidly. They can still be found in areas such as South Heaton in Newcastle but once dominated the streetscape on both sides of the Tyne.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-110) Tyneside flats were built as terraces, one of each pair of doors led to an upstairs flat while the other led into the ground-floor flat, each of two or three rooms. A new development in the Ouseburn valley has recreated them; Architects Cany Ash and Robert Sakula were attracted by the possibilities of high density without building high and getting rid of common areas.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-111)

In terms of housing stock, the authority is one of few authorities to see the proportion of detached homes rise in the 2010 Census (to 7.8%), in this instance this was coupled with a similar rise in flats and waterside apartments to 25.6%, and the proportion of converted or shared houses in 2011 renders this dwelling type within the highest of the five colour-coded brackets at 5.9%, and on a par with [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford "Oxford") and [Reading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading,_Berkshire "Reading, Berkshire"), greater than [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester") and [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool "Liverpool") and below a handful of historic densely occupied, arguably overinflated markets in the local authorities: [Harrogate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrogate "Harrogate"), [Cheltenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheltenham "Cheltenham"), [Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath,_Somerset "Bath, Somerset"), inner London, [Hastings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastings "Hastings"), [Brighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton "Brighton") and [Royal Tunbridge Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Tunbridge_Wells "Royal Tunbridge Wells").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-112)

Significant Newcastle [housing developments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_developments "Housing developments") include [Ralph Erskine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Erskine_(architect) "Ralph Erskine (architect)")'s the [Byker Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byker_Wall "Byker Wall") designed in the 1960s, and now [Grade II* listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"). It is on [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")'s list of outstanding 20th-century buildings.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-113) The Byker Redevelopment has won the first [Veronica Rudge Green Prize in Urban Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veronica_Rudge_Green_Prize_in_Urban_Design "Veronica Rudge Green Prize in Urban Design") in 1988.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-114)

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Climate")]

Newcastle has an [oceanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate") climate ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"): _[Cfb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic\_climate "Oceanic climate")_). Data in Newcastle was first collected in 1802 by the solicitor [James Losh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Losh "James Losh").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-tyneWeather1800s-115) Situated in the [rain shadow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_shadow "Rain shadow") of the [North Pennines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pennines "North Pennines"), Newcastle is amongst the driest cities in the UK. Temperature extremes recorded at Newcastle Weather Centre include 37.0°C (98.6°F) set on 19 July 2022[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-116) down to −14.0°C (6.8°F) on 29 December 1995.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-117) Newcastle can have cool to cold winters, though usually milder than the rural areas around it, and summers range from pleasant to fairly warm, with very long daylight hours in comparison to all other major English cities. Newcastle upon Tyne shares the same latitude as [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen"), southern Sweden and [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow").

Unlike more western, windward areas of the British Isles affected by heavy rain (that tends to be concentrated in the cooler months), Newcastle has less seasonal variation in rainfall, and less rainfall overall, compared to the UK average. Snowfall is not the norm and often light. Despite snowfall becoming even less frequent due to the effects of [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change"), Newcastle nevertheless receives more than most major English cities, with any given year averaging 5-10 days of lying snow.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-118)

The nearest weather station to provide sunshine statistics is at Durham, about 14 miles (23 km) south of [Newcastle City Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_City_Centre "Newcastle City Centre"). Durham's inland, less urbanised setting results in night-time temperature data about 1 degree cooler than Newcastle proper throughout the year.

### Environment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Environment")]

Main article: [North East Green Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Green_Belt "North East Green Belt")

The city is located within the centre of the North East Green Belt, also known as the Tyne and Wear Green Belt.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-122)

The green belts stated aims[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-123) are to:

*   _Prevent the merging of settlements_
*   _Safeguard the countryside from encroachment_
*   _Check unrestricted [urban sprawl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban\_sprawl "Urban sprawl")_
*   _Assist in urban regeneration in the city-region by encouraging the recycling of derelict and other urban land_

The green belt surrounds [Brunswick Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunswick_Village "Brunswick Village"), [Dinnington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinnington,_Tyne_and_Wear "Dinnington, Tyne and Wear"), Callerton, [Hazlerigg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazlerigg "Hazlerigg"), [Throckley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Throckley "Throckley"), [Walbottle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walbottle "Walbottle"), and [Woolsington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolsington "Woolsington"). Popular locations such as Ryton Island, Tyne Riverside Country Park, the city's golf courses, [Newcastle Racecourse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_Racecourse "Newcastle Racecourse"), and [Newcastle International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_International_Airport "Newcastle International Airport") fall inside the green belt.

The city has been recognised for its commitment to environmental issues, with a programme planned for Newcastle to become "the first [carbon neutral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_neutrality "Carbon neutrality") city"[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-124) however, those plans have been revised and they now hope to be carbon neutral by 2050.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-125)

## Culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Culture")]

### Nightlife

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Nightlife")]

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/The_Gate_Newcastle.jpg/250px-The_Gate_Newcastle.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Gate_Newcastle.jpg)

The Gate complex on Newgate Street is a nightlife destination.

In 2006, _The [Rough Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rough\_Guides "Rough Guides") to Britain_ placed Newcastle upon Tyne's nightlife as Great Britain's number one [tourist attraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourist_attraction "Tourist attraction").[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-rGuideNo1NLife-126) In 2010, the [Tripadvisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripadvisor "Tripadvisor") Travellers' Choice Destination Awards for Nightlife destinations, Newcastle was awarded third place in Europe (behind London and [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"))[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-tripadvisor2010-08-12-127) and seventh place in the world.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Tripadvisor2-2010-08-12-128) In July 2023, Newcastle was voted the best city in the UK for food, fashion and nightlife.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-vibesJuly2023-129)

There are many bars on the [Bigg Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bigg_Market "Bigg Market") and its adjoining streets. Other areas popular for nightlife include Collingwood Street (commonly referred to as the 'Diamond Strip' due to its concentration of high-end bars). Neville Street, the [Central Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_railway_station "Newcastle railway station") area, Osborne Road in [Jesmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesmond "Jesmond") and the wider [Ouseburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouseburn "Ouseburn") area are home to a variety of younger metropolitan bars. "[The Gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gate,_Newcastle "The Gate, Newcastle")", located on Newgate Street, has become a popular venue for late-night entertainment in the past decade and a half.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-130) Newcastle's ['pink triangle'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay_community "Gay community") is concentrated on Times Square, surrounded by the [Centre for Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Life "Centre for Life").[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-131)[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-132)

### Food

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Food")]

Bakery chain [Greggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greggs "Greggs") was founded, and is headquartered, in Newcastle and has the greatest number of Greggs stores [per capita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_capita "Per capita") in the world.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-chroniclelive4-133) Local delicacies include [pease pudding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pease_pudding "Pease pudding") and [stottie cake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stottie_cake "Stottie cake").

In 1967, London based [Smith's Crisps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Smith's_Snackfood_Company "The Smith's Snackfood Company") created Salt & Vinegar flavour crisps which were first produced by their Newcastle based subsidiary [Tudor Crisps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tudor_Crisps "Tudor Crisps") and tested in Tudor's home market of north-east England before being launched nationally.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-134)

In 2010, Osborne Road in [Jesmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesmond "Jesmond") was awarded fourth place in the UK Google Street View awards for the "foodie" category.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-google_street_view-86) Newcastle has its own [Chinatown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinatown "Chinatown").

Additionally, the city has a wide variety of cuisines available including [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_food "Greek food"), [Mexican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_food "Mexican food"), [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_food "Spanish food"), [Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_food "Indian food"), [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_food "Italian food"), [Persian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_food "Persian food"), [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_food "Japanese food"), [Malaysian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysian_food "Malaysian food"), [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_food "French food"), [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_food "American food"), [Mongolian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongolian_cuisine "Mongolian cuisine"), [Moroccan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroccan_food "Moroccan food"), [Thai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_cuisine "Thai cuisine"), [Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_food "Polish food"), [Vietnamese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnamese_cuisine "Vietnamese cuisine") and [Lebanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanese_cuisine "Lebanese cuisine"). There has also been a noticeable growth in Newcastle's [gourmet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gourmet "Gourmet") restaurant industry in recent years.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-135)[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-136)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-137)

### Theatre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Theatre")]

The city has a proud history of theatre. [Stephen Kemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Kemble "Stephen Kemble") of the well-known [Kemble family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kemble_family "Kemble family") managed the original Theatre Royal, Newcastle for fifteen years (1791–1806). He brought members of his famous acting family such as [Sarah Siddons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Siddons "Sarah Siddons") and [John Kemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Philip_Kemble "John Philip Kemble") out of London to Newcastle. Stephen Kemble guided the theatre through many celebrated seasons. The original Theatre Royal in Newcastle was opened on 21 January 1788 and was located on Mosley Street.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-theatreRoyal1788-138) It was demolished to make way for Grey Street, where its replacement was built.

**Newcastle upon Tyne**, or simply **Newcastle** ([/nj uː ˈ k æ s əl/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/1/18/En-uk-NewcastleUponTyne%28ShortA%29.ogg/En-uk-NewcastleUponTyne%28ShortA%29.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:En-uk-NewcastleUponTyne(ShortA).ogg "File:En-uk-NewcastleUponTyne(ShortA).ogg")[_new-KASS-əl_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"), [RP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Received_Pronunciation "Received Pronunciation"):[/ˈ nj uː k ɑː s əl/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/4/44/En-gb-rp-Newcastle-upon-Tyne.ogg/En-gb-rp-Newcastle-upon-Tyne.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:En-gb-rp-Newcastle-upon-Tyne.ogg "File:En-gb-rp-Newcastle-upon-Tyne.ogg")[_NEW-kah-səl_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Wells2008-4) is a [city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_status_in_the_United_Kingdom "City status in the United Kingdom") and [metropolitan borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_borough "Metropolitan borough") in [Tyne and Wear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_and_Wear "Tyne and Wear"), England. It is England's northernmost city, located on the [River Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne "River Tyne")'s northern bank opposite [Gateshead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateshead "Gateshead") to the south. It is the most populous settlement in the [Tyneside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyneside "Tyneside") conurbation and [North East England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England "North East England").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-2021census-5) The metropolitan borough had an estimated population of 320,605 in 2024.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-popstats-2)

Newcastle developed around a [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") settlement called [Pons Aelius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pons_Aelius "Pons Aelius").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-6) The settlement became known as _Monkchester_ before taking on the name of [a castle built in 1080](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Castle,_Newcastle "The Castle, Newcastle") by [William the Conqueror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_the_Conqueror "William the Conqueror")'s eldest son, [Robert Curthose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Curthose "Robert Curthose"). It was one of the world's largest [ship building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship_building "Ship building") and repair centres during the [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-7)

Newcastle was historically part of the county of [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland "Northumberland"), but governed as a [county corporate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_corporate "County corporate") after 1400.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-self57567-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-sepNewc-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-archivesMuseumSeparatedFromNorthumberland-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-countyOfItself_Separated_1400-11) In 1974, Newcastle became part of the newly created metropolitan county of Tyne and Wear. The local authority is [Newcastle City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_City_Council "Newcastle City Council"), which is a constituent member of the [North East Combined Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Combined_Authority "North East Combined Authority").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Main article: [History of Newcastle upon Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Newcastle_upon_Tyne "History of Newcastle upon Tyne")

### Roman era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Roman era")]

The first recorded settlement in what is now Newcastle was [Pons Aelius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pons_Aelius "Pons Aelius") ("Aelian bridge"), a Roman fort and bridge across the [River Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne "River Tyne"). It was given the family name of the [Roman emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Emperor "Roman Emperor")[Hadrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrian "Hadrian"), who founded it in the 2nd century AD. This rare honour suggests Hadrian may have visited the site and instituted the bridge on his tour of Britain. The population of Pons Aelius then is estimated at 2,000. Fragments of [Hadrian's Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrian's_Wall "Hadrian's Wall") are visible in parts of Newcastle, particularly along the West Road. The course of the "Roman Wall" can be traced eastwards to [Segedunum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Segedunum "Segedunum"), a [Roman fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castra "Castra") in [Wallsend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallsend "Wallsend") – the "wall's end" – and to the separate supply fort of [Arbeia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbeia "Arbeia") in [South Shields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shields "South Shields"), across the river from Hadrian's Wall.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-12)

The extent of Hadrian's Wall was 73 miles (117 km), spanning the width of Britain; the Wall incorporated the [Vallum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vallum_(Hadrian's_Wall) "Vallum (Hadrian's Wall)"), a large rearward ditch with parallel mounds,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-13) and was built primarily for defence and to prevent the incursion of [Pictish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pict "Pict") tribes from the north, and probably not as a fighting line for a major invasion. However, it seems that the Vallum stopped just west of Newcastle, where its role as a secondary line of defence was performed by the [River Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne "River Tyne").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-14)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Newcastle_schloss.jpg/250px-Newcastle_schloss.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Newcastle_schloss.jpg)

[Newcastle Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Castle,_Newcastle "The Castle, Newcastle")[Keep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep "Keep") is the oldest structure in the city,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] dating back to the 1170s.

### Anglo-Saxon and Norman eras

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Anglo-Saxon and Norman eras")]

After the [Roman departure from Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_Roman_rule_in_Britain "End of Roman rule in Britain"), completed in 410, Newcastle became part of the powerful [Anglo-Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_England "Anglo-Saxon England") kingdom of [Northumbria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumbria "Northumbria"), and was known throughout this period as _Munucceaster_ (sometimes modernised as _Monkchester_).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Monkchester-15)

Conflicts with the [Danes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danes_(Germanic_tribe) "Danes (Germanic tribe)") in 876 left the settlements along the River Tyne in ruins.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ncl.ac.uk-16) After the conflicts with the Danes, and following the [1088 rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebellion_of_1088 "Rebellion of 1088") against the Normans, Monkchester was all but destroyed by [Odo of Bayeux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odo_of_Bayeux "Odo of Bayeux").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-17)

Because of its strategic position, [Robert Curthose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Curthose "Robert Curthose"), son of [William the Conqueror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_I_of_England "William I of England"), erected a wooden [castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Castle,_Newcastle "The Castle, Newcastle") there in the year 1080.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ncl.ac.uk-16) The town was henceforth known as _Novum Castellum_ or _New Castle_.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ncl.ac.uk-16) The wooden structure was replaced by a stone castle in 1087.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ncl.ac.uk-16) The castle was rebuilt again in 1172 during the reign of Henry II. Much of the keep which can be seen in the city today dates from this period.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ncl.ac.uk-16)

### Middle Ages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Middle Ages")]

Throughout the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"), Newcastle was England's northern fortress. In 1400 Newcastle was separated from Northumberland for administrative purposes[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-self57567-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-sepNewc-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-archivesMuseumSeparatedFromNorthumberland-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-countyOfItself_Separated_1400-11) and made a [county of itself](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_itself "County of itself") by [Henry IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV_of_England "Henry IV of England").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-self57567-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-sepNewc-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-archivesMuseumSeparatedFromNorthumberland-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-countyOfItself_Separated_1400-11) Newcastle was given the title of the county of the town of Newcastle upon Tyne.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-sepNewc-9) The town had a new charter granted by [Elizabeth I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_I "Elizabeth I") in 1589.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-self57567-8) A 25-foot-high (7.6 m) stone [wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_town_wall "Newcastle town wall") was built around the town in the 13th century,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-newc13thcent-18) to defend it from invaders during the [Border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_country "Border country") war against Scotland. The Scots king [William the Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_the_Lion "William the Lion") was imprisoned in Newcastle in 1174, and [Edward I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_I_of_England "Edward I of England") brought the [Stone of Scone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_of_Scone "Stone of Scone") and [William Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wallace "William Wallace") south through the town. Newcastle was successfully defended against the Scots three times during the 14th century.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-self57567-8)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-countyOfItself_Separated_1400-11)

### 16th to 19th centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 16th to 19th centuries")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Newcastle-upon-Tyne_from_New_Chatham_engraving_by_William_Miller_after_T_Allom.jpg/330px-Newcastle-upon-Tyne_from_New_Chatham_engraving_by_William_Miller_after_T_Allom.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Newcastle-upon-Tyne_from_New_Chatham_engraving_by_William_Miller_after_T_Allom.jpg)

An engraving by [William Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Miller_(engraver) "William Miller (engraver)") of Newcastle in 1832, as seen from [Gateshead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateshead "Gateshead")

From 1530, a royal act restricted all shipments of coal from [Tyneside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyneside "Tyneside") to [Newcastle Quayside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_Quayside "Newcastle Quayside"), giving a monopoly in the coal trade to a cartel of Newcastle burgesses known as the [Hostmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hostmen_of_Newcastle-upon-Tyne "The Hostmen of Newcastle-upon-Tyne"). This monopoly, which lasted for a considerable time, helped Newcastle prosper and develop into a major town. The phrase _[taking coals to Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coals\_to\_Newcastle "Coals to Newcastle")_ was first recorded contextually in 1538.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-coalsNewcastle-19) The phrase itself means a pointless pursuit.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-coalsToNewcastle-20) In the 18th century, the American entrepreneur [Timothy Dexter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Dexter "Timothy Dexter"), regarded as an eccentric, defied this idiom. He was persuaded to sail a shipment of coal to Newcastle by merchants plotting to ruin him; however, his shipment arrived on the Tyne during a strike that had crippled local production, allowing him to turn a considerable profit.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-knapp-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-nash-22)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Victoria_Tunnel_%28Newcastle%29_near_Ouse_Street_2010-02-19.jpg/250px-Victoria_Tunnel_%28Newcastle%29_near_Ouse_Street_2010-02-19.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Victoria_Tunnel_(Newcastle)_near_Ouse_Street_2010-02-19.jpg)

Victoria Tunnel, built to transport coal

[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-VTunnel201401-23)

In the Sandgate area, to the east of the city, and beside the river, resided the close-knit community of [keelmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keelmen "Keelmen") and their families.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-keelmen-24) They were so called because they worked on the keels, boats that were used to transfer coal from the river banks to the waiting [colliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collier_(ship) "Collier (ship)"), for export to London and elsewhere. In the 1630s, about 7,000 out of 20,000 inhabitants of Newcastle died of [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death_in_England "Black Death in England"), more than one-third of the population.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-25) Specifically within the year 1636, it is roughly estimated with evidence held by the [Society of Antiquaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Antiquaries_of_Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Society of Antiquaries of Newcastle upon Tyne") that 47% of the then population of Newcastle died from the epidemic; this may also have been the most devastating loss in any British city in this period.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Plag1636-26)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/The_Quayside%2C_Newcastle_upon_Tyne%2C_1961_%2815657916212%29.jpg/250px-The_Quayside%2C_Newcastle_upon_Tyne%2C_1961_%2815657916212%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Quayside,_Newcastle_upon_Tyne,_1961_(15657916212).jpg)

Newcastle was once a major industrial centre, particularly for coal and shipping.

During the [English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War"), the North declared for the King.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-northCWar-27) In a bid to gain Newcastle and the Tyne, [Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell")'s allies, the Scots, captured the town of [Newburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newburn "Newburn"). In 1644, the Scots then captured the reinforced fortification on the Lawe in [South Shields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shields "South Shields") following a siege and the city was [besieged for many months](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Newcastle "Siege of Newcastle"). It was eventually stormed ("with roaring drummes") and sacked by Cromwell's allies. The grateful King bestowed the [motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motto "Motto")_Fortiter Defendit Triumphans_ ([Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language") for 'Triumphing by a brave defence') upon the town. Charles I was imprisoned in Newcastle by the Scots in 1646–47.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-civilWar-28)

After the [Union in 1707](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_Union_1707 "Acts of Union 1707"), the City walls became obsolete, and gave way to an expansion of the city[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-29). Despite the Jacobite [risings of 1715](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobite_rising_of_1715 "Jacobite rising of 1715") and [1745](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobite_rising_of_1745 "Jacobite rising of 1745"), fortifications gave way to industrial development.

The extraction and processing of coal and iron created a series of specialised industries, such as steel manufacture and eventually steam power.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-30)

Newcastle also became a glass producer with a reputation for brilliant [flint glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flint_glass "Flint glass").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-31) Glass was key in the industrial development of the Tyne and Wear region.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-32)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Newcastle_City_Centre_17.9.1917.jpg/250px-Newcastle_City_Centre_17.9.1917.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Newcastle_City_Centre_17.9.1917.jpg)

Newcastle city centre, 1917, with St James' Park football ground above and left of centre

Newcastle opened its first [lunatic asylum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunatic_asylum "Lunatic asylum") in 1767.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-lunaticAsylum1767-33) The asylum catered for people from the counties of Newcastle, Durham and Northumberland.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-lunaticAsylum1767-33)

[The Newcastle Eccentrics of the 19th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Newcastle_Eccentrics_of_the_19th_century "The Newcastle Eccentrics of the 19th century") were a group of unrelated people who lived in and around the centre of Newcastle and its Quayside between the end of the 18th and early/mid 19th century. They are depicted in a painting by [Henry Perlee Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Perlee_Parker "Henry Perlee Parker").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-34)

Newcastle was the country's fourth largest print centre after London, [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford "Oxford") and [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge "Cambridge"),[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-pPressNewc-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-printPNewc1710-36) and the [Literary and Philosophical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_and_Philosophical_Society "Literary and Philosophical Society") of 1793,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-printing2010-07-26-37) with its erudite debates and large stock of books in several languages, predated the [London Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Library "London Library") by half a century.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-printing2010-07-26-37) Some founder members of the [Literary and Philosophical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_and_Philosophical_Society "Literary and Philosophical Society") were abolitionists.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-litPhil-38)[_[self-published source?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Self-published\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

A permanent military presence was established in the city with the completion of [Fenham Barracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenham_Barracks "Fenham Barracks") in 1806.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-history-39)

The [great fire of Newcastle and Gateshead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_fire_of_Newcastle_and_Gateshead "Great fire of Newcastle and Gateshead") was a tragic and spectacular series of events starting on Friday 6 October 1854, in which a substantial amount of property in the two North East of England towns was destroyed in a series of fires and an explosion which killed 53 and injured hundreds.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-40)

The status of city was granted to Newcastle on 3 June 1882.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-41) In the 19th century, [shipbuilding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shipbuilding "Shipbuilding") and [heavy engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Newcastle_upon_Tyne#Locomotive_manufacture "History of Newcastle upon Tyne") were central to the city's prosperity; and the city was a powerhouse of the [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-IndRev201401-42) This revolution resulted in the urbanisation of the city.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Urb2014-01-43) In 1817, the Maling company, at one time the largest pottery company in the world, moved to the city.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-pottery-44) The Victorian industrial revolution brought industrial structures that included the 2+1⁄2-mile (4 km)[Victoria Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Tunnel_(Newcastle) "Victoria Tunnel (Newcastle)"), built in 1842, which provided underground wagon ways to the [staithes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jetty "Jetty").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-VTunnel2014012-45) On 3 February 1879, Mosley Street in the city, was the first public road in the world to be lit up by the [incandescent lightbulb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_light "Street light").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-jswan2014061-46)[_[self-published source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Self-published\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_][[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-jswan2014062-47) Newcastle was one of the first cities in the world to be lit up by electric lighting.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Mosely-48)

Innovations in Newcastle and surrounding areas included the development of [safety lamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davy_lamp "Davy lamp"), [Stephenson's Rocket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephenson's_Rocket "Stephenson's Rocket"), [Lord Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_George_Armstrong "William George Armstrong")'s artillery, [Be-Ro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Be-Ro "Be-Ro") flour,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-bero2011-49)[Lucozade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucozade "Lucozade"),[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-50)[Joseph Swan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Swan "Joseph Swan")'s [electric light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_light "Electric light") bulbs, and [Charles Parsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Algernon_Parsons "Charles Algernon Parsons")' invention of the [steam turbine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_turbine "Steam turbine"), which led to the revolution of marine propulsion and the production of [cheap electricity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_generator "Electrical generator"). In 1882, Newcastle became the seat of an [Anglican diocese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_of_Newcastle "Diocese of Newcastle"), with [St. Nicholas' Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_Cathedral "Newcastle Cathedral") becoming its cathedral.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Cathedral1882-51)

### 20th and 21st centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 20th and 21st centuries")]

Newcastle's public transport system was modernised in 1901 when [Newcastle Corporation Tramways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_Corporation_Tramways "Newcastle Corporation Tramways") electric trams were introduced to the city's streets, though these were replaced gradually by trolley buses from 1935, with the tram service finally coming to an end in 1950.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-transport1901-1950-52)

The city acquired its first art gallery, the [Laing Art Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laing_Art_Gallery "Laing Art Gallery") in 1904, so named after its founder Alexander Laing, a Scottish wine and spirit merchant[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-alexanderLaing13Oct1904-53) who wanted to give something back to the city in which he had made his fortune. Another art gallery – founded in 1926 by the King Edward VII School of Art – is the [Hatton Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatton_Gallery "Hatton Gallery"), which is now part of [Newcastle University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University "Newcastle University").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-hattonGallery1925_1-54)

With the advent of the motor car, Newcastle's road network was improved in the early part of the 20th century, beginning with the opening of the Redheugh road bridge in 1901[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-redheughBridge1901-55) and the [Tyne Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_Bridge "Tyne Bridge") in 1928.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-tyneBridge1928-56)

Efforts to preserve the city's historic past were evident as long ago as 1934, when the Museum of Science and Industry opened,[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-57) as did the [John G Joicey Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Jesus_Hospital#The_first_museum:_The_John_George_Joicey_Museum_(1950%E2%80%931993) "Holy Jesus Hospital") in the same year.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-58)

[Council housing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_housing "Council housing") began to replace inner-city slums in the 1920s, and the process continued into the 1970s, along with substantial private house building and acquisitions.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-59)

Unemployment hit record heights in Newcastle during the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") of the 1930s. The city's last coal pit closed in 1956,[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-openCastSciCity2011-60) though a temporary open cast mine was opened in 2013.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-openCastSciCity2013-61) The temporary open cast mine shifted 40,000 tonnes of coal, using modern techniques to reduce noise, on a part of the City undergoing redevelopment.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-openCastSciCity2013-61) The slow demise of the shipyards on the banks of the [River Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne "River Tyne") happened in the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-62)

During the Second World War, the city and surrounding area were a target for air raids as heavy industry was involved in the production of ships and armaments. The raids caused 141 deaths and 587 injuries.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-63) A former French consul in Newcastle, Jacques Serre, assisted the German war effort by describing important targets in the region to [Admiral Raeder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erich_Raeder "Erich Raeder") who was the head of the German Navy.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-64)

The public sector in Newcastle began to expand in the 1960s. The federal structure of the [University of Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Durham "University of Durham") was dissolved. That university's college in Newcastle, which had been known as King's College, became the University of Newcastle upon Tyne (now known as [Newcastle University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University "Newcastle University")), which was founded in 1963,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-65) followed by Newcastle Polytechnic in 1969; the latter received university status in 1992 and became the University of Northumbria at Newcastle (now known as [Northumbria University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumbria_University "Northumbria University")).[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-66)

Further efforts to preserve the city's historic past continued in the later 20th century, with the opening of Newcastle Military Vehicle Museum in 1983 and [Stephenson Railway Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Tyneside_Steam_Railway "North Tyneside Steam Railway") in 1986. The Military Vehicle museum closed in 2006.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-67) New developments at the turn of the 21st century included the [Life Science Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Life "Centre for Life") in 2000 and [Millennium Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateshead_Millennium_Bridge "Gateshead Millennium Bridge") in 2001.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-68)

Based at [St James' Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James'_Park "St James' Park") since 1886, [Newcastle United F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_United_F.C. "Newcastle United F.C.") became [Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League "Football League") members in 1893.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-69) They have won four top division titles (the first in 1905 and the most recent in 1927), six [FA Cups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Cup "FA Cup") (the first in 1910 and the most recent in 1955), the [Inter-Cities Fairs Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-Cities_Fairs_Cup "Inter-Cities Fairs Cup") in 1969 and most recently the [League Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EFL_Cup "EFL Cup") in 2025, their first domestic trophy since 1955.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-70) They broke the world transfer record in 1996 by paying £15 million for [Blackburn Rovers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackburn_Rovers_F.C. "Blackburn Rovers F.C.") and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_national_football_team "England national football team") striker [Alan Shearer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Shearer "Alan Shearer"), one of the most prolific goalscorers of that era.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-71)

In 2017, Newcastle was the venue for the 2017 Freedom City festival. The 2017 Freedom City festival commemorated the 50 years since [Martin Luther King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr.")'s visit to Newcastle, where King received his honorary degree from [Newcastle University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University "Newcastle University").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-freedomCity2017_1-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-honDegreeKing-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-freedomCity-74) In 2018, Newcastle hosted [the Great Exhibition of the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Exhibition_of_the_North "The Great Exhibition of the North"), the largest event in England in 2018. The exhibition began on 22 June with an opening ceremony on the River Tyne, and ended on 9 September with the [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run") weekend. The exhibition describes the story of the north of England through its innovators, artists, designers and businesses.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-riverCeremonyOpeninExh2018-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-exOfNorth2018-76)

In 2019, a travel site named Newcastle to be the friendliest city in the UK.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-chroniclelive-77)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Side_-_Tyne_Bridge.jpg/250px-Side_-_Tyne_Bridge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Side_-_Tyne_Bridge.jpg)

Side, a street in Newcastle near the Tyne Bridge

Since 1974, Newcastle has been a part of the [metropolitan county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_county "Metropolitan county") of [Tyne and Wear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_and_Wear "Tyne and Wear") in [North East England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England "North East England"). The city is located on the north-western bank of the [River Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne "River Tyne"), approximately 46 miles (74 km) south of the border with Scotland.

The ground beneath the city is formed from [Carboniferous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carboniferous "Carboniferous")[strata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratum "Stratum") of the Middle Pennine Coal Measures Group — a suite of [sandstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone"), [mudstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudstone "Mudstone") and [coal seams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_seam "Coal seam") which generally dip moderately eastwards. To the west of the city are the Upper Pennine Coal Measures and further west again the sandstones and mudstones of the Stainmore Formation, the local equivalent of the [Millstone Grit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millstone_Grit "Millstone Grit").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-78)

In large parts, Newcastle still retains a [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval "Medieval") street layout. Narrow alleys or '[chares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chare "Chare")', most of which can only be traversed by foot, still exist in abundance, particularly around the [riverside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quayside "Quayside"). Stairs from the riverside to higher parts of the city centre and the extant [Castle Keep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_Castle_Keep "Newcastle Castle Keep"), originally recorded in the 14th century, remain intact in places. Close, Sandhill and [Quayside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quayside "Quayside") contain modern buildings as well as structures dating from the 15th–18th centuries, including [Bessie Surtees House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Surtees_House "Bessie Surtees House"), the Cooperage and Lloyds Quayside Bars, Derwentwater House and House of Tides, a restaurant situated at a Grade I-listed 16th century merchant's house at 28–30 Close.

The city has an extensive [neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") centre referred to as Tyneside Classical,[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Tyneside_Classical-79) largely developed in the 1830s by [Richard Grainger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Grainger "Richard Grainger") and [John Dobson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dobson_(architect) "John Dobson (architect)"). More recently, Newcastle architecture considered to be Tyneside classical has been extensively restored. Broadcaster and writer [Stuart Maconie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Maconie "Stuart Maconie") described Newcastle as England's best-looking city[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-81) and the German-born British scholar of architecture, [Nikolaus Pevsner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolaus_Pevsner "Nikolaus Pevsner"),[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Pevsner2010-07-26-82) describes [Grey Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey_Street,_Newcastle "Grey Street, Newcastle") as one of the finest streets in England. In 1948, the poet [John Betjeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Betjeman "John Betjeman") said of Grey Street, "As for the curve of Grey Street, I shall never forget seeing it to perfection, traffic-less on a misty Sunday morning."[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-greyStBetjeman-83) The street curves down from [Grey's Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey's_Monument "Grey's Monument") towards the valley of the [River Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne,_England "River Tyne, England") and was voted England's finest street in 2005 in a survey of [BBC Radio 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_4 "BBC Radio 4") listeners.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-85) In the Google Street View awards of 2010, Grey Street came 3rd in the British picturesque category.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-google_street_view-86) A portion of [Grainger Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grainger_Town "Grainger Town") was demolished in the 1960s to make way for the [Eldon Square Shopping Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldon_Square_Shopping_Centre "Eldon Square Shopping Centre"), including all but one side of the original [Eldon Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Eldon_Square "Old Eldon Square") itself.
