Immediately to the north-west of the city centre is [Leazes Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leazes_Park "Leazes Park"), first opened to the public in 1873[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-87) after a petition by 3,000 working men of the city for "ready access to some open ground for the purpose of health and recreation". Just outside one corner of this is [St James' Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James'_Park "St James' Park"), the stadium home of [Newcastle United FC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_United_FC "Newcastle United FC") which dominates the view of the city from all directions.

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/St_James_Park_Newcastle_as_seen_from_south_of_the_River_Tyne.jpg/500px-St_James_Park_Newcastle_as_seen_from_south_of_the_River_Tyne.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_James_Park_Newcastle_as_seen_from_south_of_the_River_Tyne.jpg)

View of [St James' Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James'_Park "St James' Park") on the skyline and surrounding buildings, as seen from Gateshead

Another major [green space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_belt "Green belt") in the city is the [Town Moor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_Moor,_Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Town Moor, Newcastle upon Tyne"), lying immediately north of the city centre. It is larger than London's [Hyde Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park,_London "Hyde Park, London") and [Hampstead Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampstead_Heath "Hampstead Heath") put together[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-townmoo1-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-townmoo2-89) and the [freemen of the city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_City "Freedom of the City") have the right to graze cattle on it.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-townmoo1-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-townmoo2-89) The right extends to the pitch of [St. James' Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._James'_Park "St. James' Park"), [Newcastle United Football Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_United "Newcastle United")'s ground; this is not exercised, although the Freemen do collect rent for the loss of privilege. Honorary freemen include [Bob Geldof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Geldof "Bob Geldof"),[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-BobGeldof2010-09-17-90)[King Harald V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Harald_V "King Harald V") of Norway,[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-KingHNorway-91)[Bobby Robson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Robson "Bobby Robson"),[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-SirBobby2010-09-17-92)[Alan Shearer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Shearer "Alan Shearer"),[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-AlanShearer2010-09-17-93) the late [Nelson Mandela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela")[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Mandela2010-09-17-94) and the [Royal Shakespeare Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Shakespeare_Company "Royal Shakespeare Company").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-RoyalShakespeare-95)[The Hoppings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hoppings "The Hoppings") funfair, said to be the largest [travelling funfair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travelling_funfair "Travelling funfair") in Europe, is held here annually in June.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Hop2010-09-17-96)

In the south-eastern corner of the Town Moor is [Exhibition Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exhibition_Park,_Newcastle "Exhibition Park, Newcastle"), which contains the only remaining pavilion from the [North East Coast Exhibition of 1929](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Coast_Exhibition "North East Coast Exhibition"). From the 1970s until 2006, this housed the Newcastle Military Vehicle Museum; which closed in 2006. The pavilion is now being used as a [microbrewery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microbrewery "Microbrewery") and concert venue for [Wylam Brewery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wylam_Brewery "Wylam Brewery").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-97)

### Ouseburn

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Ouseburn")]

The wooded gorge of the [Ouseburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouseburn "Ouseburn") in the east of the city is known as [Jesmond Dene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesmond_Dene "Jesmond Dene") and forms another recreation area, linked by Armstrong Park and Heaton Park to the [Ouseburn Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouseburn_Valley "Ouseburn Valley"), where the river finally reaches the [River Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne,_England "River Tyne, England").

The springtime [dawn chorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn_chorus_(birds) "Dawn chorus (birds)") at 55 degrees latitude has been described as one of the best in the world.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-dawnChorus-98) The dawn chorus of the Jesmond Dene green space has been professionally recorded and has been used in various workplace and hospital rehabilitation facilities.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-dawnChorus-98)

### Quayside

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Quayside")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Quayside%2C_Newcastle_upon_Tyne.jpg/250px-Quayside%2C_Newcastle_upon_Tyne.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Quayside,_Newcastle_upon_Tyne.jpg)

Quayside architecture, showing the historic [Newcastle Guildhall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guildhall,_Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Guildhall, Newcastle upon Tyne") with its white turret

The area around the [Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne "River Tyne") Gorge, between Newcastle on the north bank and [Gateshead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateshead "Gateshead") on the south bank, is the famous Newcastle-Gateshead [Quayside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quayside "Quayside"). It is famed for its series of dramatic bridges, including the [Tyne Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_Bridge "Tyne Bridge") of 1928 which was built by [Dorman Long](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorman_Long "Dorman Long") of [Middlesbrough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesbrough "Middlesbrough"), [Robert Stephenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Stephenson "Robert Stephenson")'s [High Level Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Level_Bridge,_River_Tyne "High Level Bridge, River Tyne") of 1849, the first road/rail bridge in the world, and the [Swing Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_Bridge,_River_Tyne "Swing Bridge, River Tyne") of 1876.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-99)

Large-scale [regeneration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_renewal "Urban renewal") efforts have led to the replacement of former shipping premises with new office developments; a tilting bridge - the [Gateshead Millennium Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateshead_Millennium_Bridge "Gateshead Millennium Bridge") - integrated the Quayside more closely with the Gateshead Quayside, home to the [BALTIC Centre for Contemporary Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BALTIC_Centre_for_Contemporary_Art "BALTIC Centre for Contemporary Art") (the venue for the [Turner Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turner_Prize "Turner Prize") 2011)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-TurnerPrize2010-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-101) and the [Norman Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Foster,_Baron_Foster_of_Thames_Bank "Norman Foster, Baron Foster of Thames Bank")-designed [Glasshouse International Centre for Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasshouse_International_Centre_for_Music "Glasshouse International Centre for Music"). The Newcastle and Gateshead Quaysides are now a cosmopolitan area with bars, restaurants, hotels and public spaces.

### Grainger Town

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Grainger Town")]

Main article: [Grainger Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grainger_Town "Grainger Town")

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b1/Newcastle_England%2C_Grainger_Street_c._1906.jpg/250px-Newcastle_England%2C_Grainger_Street_c._1906.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Newcastle_England,_Grainger_Street_c._1906.jpg)

Grainger Street, circa 1906

The historic heart of Newcastle is the Grainger Town area. Established on classical streets built by [Richard Grainger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Grainger "Richard Grainger"), a builder and developer, between 1835 and 1842, some of Newcastle upon Tyne's finest buildings and streets lie within this area of the city centre including [Grainger Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grainger_Market "Grainger Market"), [Theatre Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_Royal,_Newcastle "Theatre Royal, Newcastle"), [Grey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_grey "Earl grey") Street, Grainger Street and [Clayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Clayton_(town_clerk) "John Clayton (town clerk)") Street.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) These buildings are predominantly four stories high, with vertical dormers, domes, turrets and spikes. Richard Grainger was said to 'have found Newcastle of bricks and timber and left it in stone'.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) Of Grainger Town's 450 buildings, 244 are [listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"), of which 29 are grade I and 49 are grade II*.

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Earl_Grey_atop_his_monument_%28geograph_2368405%29.jpg/250px-Earl_Grey_atop_his_monument_%28geograph_2368405%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Earl_Grey_atop_his_monument_(geograph_2368405).jpg)

Grey's Monument

[Grey's Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey's_Monument "Grey's Monument"), which commemorates Prime Minister [Earl Grey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Grey,_2nd_Earl_Grey "Charles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey") and his [Reform Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Act_1832 "Reform Act 1832") of 1832, stands above [Monument Metro station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_metro_station "Monument metro station") and was designed and built by [Edward Hodges Baily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Hodges_Baily "Edward Hodges Baily") and [Benjamin Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_and_Benjamin_Green "John and Benjamin Green"). Hodges, who also built [Nelson's Column](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson's_Column "Nelson's Column"), designed and built the statue,[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Baily2010-2010-07-26-104) and the monument plinth was designed and built by Benjamin Green.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-BenjaminGreen2010-07-26-105)

The Grainger Market replaced an earlier market originally built in 1808 called the Butcher Market.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Grain201308-106) The Grainger Market was Newcastle's first indoor market.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) At the time of its opening in 1835, it was said to be one of the largest and most beautiful markets in Europe.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) The opening was celebrated with a grand dinner attended by 2000 guests, and the Laing Art Gallery has a painting of this event.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) With the exception of the timber roof which was destroyed by a fire in 1901 and replaced by latticed-steel arches the Market is largely in its original condition.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) The Grainger Market architecture, like most in Grainger Town, which are either grade I or II listed, was listed grade I in 1954 by English Heritage.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Grain201308-106)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-107)

The development of the city in the 1960s saw the demolition of part of [Grainger Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grainger_Town "Grainger Town") as a prelude to the modernist rebuilding initiatives of [T. Dan Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._Dan_Smith "T. Dan Smith"), the leader of [Newcastle City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_City_Council "Newcastle City Council"). A corruption scandal was uncovered involving Smith and [John Poulson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Poulson "John Poulson"), a [property developer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate_developer "Real estate developer") from [Pontefract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontefract "Pontefract"), West Yorkshire, and both were imprisoned. Echoes of the scandal were revisited in the late 1990s in the [BBC TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_TV "BBC TV") series, _[Our Friends in the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Our\_Friends\_in\_the\_North "Our Friends in the North")_.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-108)

### Housing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Housing")]

The [Tyneside flat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyneside_flat "Tyneside flat") was the dominant housing form constructed at the time when the industrial centres on Tyneside were growing most rapidly. They can still be found in areas such as South Heaton in Newcastle but once dominated the streetscape on both sides of the Tyne.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-110) Tyneside flats were built as terraces, one of each pair of doors led to an upstairs flat while the other led into the ground-floor flat, each of two or three rooms. A new development in the Ouseburn valley has recreated them; Architects Cany Ash and Robert Sakula were attracted by the possibilities of high density without building high and getting rid of common areas.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-111)

In terms of housing stock, the authority is one of few authorities to see the proportion of detached homes rise in the 2010 Census (to 7.8%), in this instance this was coupled with a similar rise in flats and waterside apartments to 25.6%, and the proportion of converted or shared houses in 2011 renders this dwelling type within the highest of the five colour-coded brackets at 5.9%, and on a par with [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford "Oxford") and [Reading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading,_Berkshire "Reading, Berkshire"), greater than [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester") and [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool "Liverpool") and below a handful of historic densely occupied, arguably overinflated markets in the local authorities: [Harrogate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrogate "Harrogate"), [Cheltenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheltenham "Cheltenham"), [Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath,_Somerset "Bath, Somerset"), inner London, [Hastings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastings "Hastings"), [Brighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton "Brighton") and [Royal Tunbridge Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Tunbridge_Wells "Royal Tunbridge Wells").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-112)

Significant Newcastle [housing developments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_developments "Housing developments") include [Ralph Erskine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Erskine_(architect) "Ralph Erskine (architect)")'s the [Byker Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byker_Wall "Byker Wall") designed in the 1960s, and now [Grade II* listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"). It is on [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")'s list of outstanding 20th-century buildings.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-113) The Byker Redevelopment has won the first [Veronica Rudge Green Prize in Urban Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veronica_Rudge_Green_Prize_in_Urban_Design "Veronica Rudge Green Prize in Urban Design") in 1988.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-114)

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Climate")]

Newcastle has an [oceanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate") climate ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"): _[Cfb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic\_climate "Oceanic climate")_). Data in Newcastle was first collected in 1802 by the solicitor [James Losh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Losh "James Losh").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-tyneWeather1800s-115) Situated in the [rain shadow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_shadow "Rain shadow") of the [North Pennines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pennines "North Pennines"), Newcastle is amongst the driest cities in the UK. Temperature extremes recorded at Newcastle Weather Centre include 37.0°C (98.6°F) set on 19 July 2022[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-116) down to −14.0°C (6.8°F) on 29 December 1995.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-117) Newcastle can have cool to cold winters, though usually milder than the rural areas around it, and summers range from pleasant to fairly warm, with very long daylight hours in comparison to all other major English cities. Newcastle upon Tyne shares the same latitude as [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen"), southern Sweden and [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow").

Unlike more western, windward areas of the British Isles affected by heavy rain (that tends to be concentrated in the cooler months), Newcastle has less seasonal variation in rainfall, and less rainfall overall, compared to the UK average. Snowfall is not the norm and often light. Despite snowfall becoming even less frequent due to the effects of [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change"), Newcastle nevertheless receives more than most major English cities, with any given year averaging 5-10 days of lying snow.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-118)

The nearest weather station to provide sunshine statistics is at Durham, about 14 miles (23 km) south of [Newcastle City Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_City_Centre "Newcastle City Centre"). Durham's inland, less urbanised setting results in night-time temperature data about 1 degree cooler than Newcastle proper throughout the year.

### Environment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Environment")]

Main article: [North East Green Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Green_Belt "North East Green Belt")

The city is located within the centre of the North East Green Belt, also known as the Tyne and Wear Green Belt.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-122)

The green belts stated aims[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-123) are to:

*   _Prevent the merging of settlements_
*   _Safeguard the countryside from encroachment_
*   _Check unrestricted [urban sprawl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban\_sprawl "Urban sprawl")_
*   _Assist in urban regeneration in the city-region by encouraging the recycling of derelict and other urban land_

The green belt surrounds [Brunswick Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunswick_Village "Brunswick Village"), [Dinnington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinnington,_Tyne_and_Wear "Dinnington, Tyne and Wear"), Callerton, [Hazlerigg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazlerigg "Hazlerigg"), [Throckley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Throckley "Throckley"), [Walbottle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walbottle "Walbottle"), and [Woolsington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolsington "Woolsington"). Popular locations such as Ryton Island, Tyne Riverside Country Park, the city's golf courses, [Newcastle Racecourse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_Racecourse "Newcastle Racecourse"), and [Newcastle International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_International_Airport "Newcastle International Airport") fall inside the green belt.

The city has been recognised for its commitment to environmental issues, with a programme planned for Newcastle to become "the first [carbon neutral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_neutrality "Carbon neutrality") city"[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-124) however, those plans have been revised and they now hope to be carbon neutral by 2050.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-125)

The 2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum took place in the United Kingdom and Gibraltar on 23 June 2016.[1][2] Membership of the European Union had been a topic of political debate in the United Kingdom since the country joined the European Communities (then commonly referred to as the "Common Market" by the British people) in 1973. This referendum was conducted very differently from the European Communities membership referendum in 1975; a more localised and regionalised counting procedure was used, and the ballot was overseen by the Electoral Commission, a public body that did not exist at the time of the first vote. This article lists, by voting area for Great Britain and Gibraltar and by parliamentary constituency for Northern Ireland, all the results of the referendum, each ordered into national and regional sections.

Under the provisions of the European Union Referendum Act 2015, there were a total of 382 voting areas across twelve regions, using the same boundaries as used in European Parliamentary elections since 1999, under the provisions of the European Parliamentary Elections Act 2002, with votes counted at local authority level. In England the 326 local government districts were used as the voting areas; these consist of all unitary authorities, all metropolitan boroughs, all shire districts, the London boroughs, the City of London and the Isles of Scilly.[3] The nine regions of England were then also used to count the votes at the regional level, with Gibraltar being regarded as part of South West England. Northern Ireland was a single voting area as well as being a regional count, although local totals by Westminster parliamentary constituency area were announced.[3] In Scotland the 32 Scottish council areas were used as voting areas, and there was a single national count.[3] In Wales the 22 Welsh council areas were used as the voting areas, and there was a single national count.[3]

Verification and counting began as soon as the polls closed on 23 June from 22:00 BST onwards (making it the first UK-wide referendum to be counted overnight) and took nine hours and twenty minutes to complete. The early results showed at different times narrow leads for both Remain and Leave; however, Leave took the lead in the national vote count for the final time at 02:58 BST when Castle Point declared its result. The result of the referendum was forecast by the BBC just before 04:40 BST (around 6 hours 40 minutes after polls closed), with around 308 results declared at the time. The first result announced was Gibraltar, and the last was Cornwall.

On 24 June 2016, the recorded result was that the UK voted to leave the European Union by 51.89% for Leave to 48.11% for Remain, a margin of 3.78%. This corresponded to 17,410,742 votes to leave and 16,141,241 to remain, a margin of 1,269,501 votes.

United Kingdomedit
Of the 382 voting areas in Great Britain and Gibraltar and the 18 Northern Ireland parliamentary constituencies, a total of 270 returned "majority" votes in favour of "Leave the European Union", while 129 returned "majority" votes in favour of "Remain a member of the European Union", including all 32 voting areas in Scotland.
  Leave
  Remain

The final result of the referendum for the United Kingdom and Gibraltar was declared at Manchester Town Hall at 0720 BST on Friday 24 June 2016, after all the 382 voting areas and the twelve UK regions had declared their results, by the Chief Counting Officer (CCO) for the referendum, Jenny Watson. In a UK-wide referendum the position of CCO is held by the chair of the Electoral Commission.[4] The following figures are as reported by the Electoral Commission.[5]

"Leave the European Union" secured a majority of 1,269,501 votes (3.78%) over those who had voted in favour of "Remain a member of the European Union". England (except Greater London) and Wales voted to "Leave", while Scotland and Northern Ireland voted to "Remain".

Results from the 30 largest cities in the United Kingdomedit

Out of over 33.5 million valid votes cast across the United Kingdom, over 8.8 million, or just over one quarter, were cast in thirty major cities that each gathered 100,000 votes or more. 16 of those cities voted to Leave, and 14 voted to Remain, or 53% Leave and 47% Remain.

In those 30 cities, votes to Remain outnumbered those to Leave by over 900,000 (about 4.9 million to 4 million or 55.2% to 44.8%), while in the other voting areas, the votes to Leave outnumbered those to Remain by nearly 2.2 million (about 13.5 million to 11.3 million, or 54.4% to 45.6%).

While all council counting areas showed a majority to remain, one constituency, Banff and Buchan, voted to leave by an estimated ratio of 54% to 46%.[8][9] Voting to leave the EU was most concentrated around the north coast of Aberdeenshire between the fishing towns of Banff and Peterhead, where there were 23,707 Leave votes to 14,918 Remain votes (61% Leave 39% Remain).[10]

The areas of Whalsay and South Unst in the Shetland Islands and An Taobh Siar and Nis in Na h-Eileanan an Iar (The Western Isles) also voted by a majority for Leave,[11] as did the town of Lossiemouth in Moray.[12][13]

The Welsh council areas were used as the voting areas for the referendum throughout Wales.

A total of 650,000 inhabitants born in England live in Wales (21%), with the areas with the highest percentages voting to leave.[14] The majority to leave the EU was 82,000.[14] The map shows council areas comprising ex-heavy industrial places and English-speaking as a common preference as areas where Leave won out. Parts of rural Wales also saw a leave-vote majority (but also Anglesey where Welsh is just as commonly if not more usually spoken). Cardiff, the Plaid Cymru heartland of the two council areas in West Wales, and by wafer-thin margins affluent Monmouthshire and the Vale of Glamorgan were the areas where Remain held sway.

The narrowest margin of victory for any of the 382 voting areas in the United Kingdom was in the Scottish council area of Moray, which voted by just 122 votes or 0.25% margin in favour of Remain.

In England the narrowest margins of victory for Leave were in Watford which voted by just 252 votes or 0.54% margin in favour of Leave, and in Cherwell which voted by just 500 votes or 0.61% margin in favour of Leave. The narrowest margin of victory for Remain was in the London Borough of Bromley, which voted by just 2,364 votes or a 1.30% margin in favour of Remain.

The area with the closest vote to the national result of 51.89% for Leave, was Basingstoke and Deane, where 51.90% of people voted Leave.

Turnout by age groupedit

After the referendum, the annual British Social Attitudes survey questioned the public on their participation. Interviewing was mainly carried out between July and October 2016 and respondents were subdivided into three age groups (18–34, 35–64 and >/=65).[17] The survey revealed that turnout was higher in the older age groups, and was 64%, 80% and 89% respectively. The age disparity had also been a feature of previous elections and referendums. However, compared to the previous referendum in 2011, the young voters' turnout in 2016 had increased sharply by 31%, while turnout by the two older age categories had also increased, but only by 26% and 21%.

Irregularitiesedit
See also: Russian interference in the 2016 Brexit referendum

In July 2018, Vote Leave was found by the Electoral Commission to have broken electoral law, spending over its limit.[18] Connected to this, the Information Commissioner's Office found that data had been unlawfully harvested from UK voters, and issued a notice of intent to fine Facebook £500,000.[19] Also, the House of Commons Culture, Media and Sport Select Committee, released an interim report on "Disinformation and 'fake news'", stating that Russia had engaged in "unconventional warfare" through Twitter and other social media against the United Kingdom, designed to amplify support for a "leave" vote in Brexit. It also found that it could not be satisfied that the largest donor in the Brexit campaign, Arron Banks, used money from UK sources, and found that he might have been financed by the Russian government.[20] This led to litigation to declare the result void.[21] Kyle Taylor of the Fair Vote Project, a campaign group that called for a public inquiry and supported a second referendum, said: "The issue is too big to have half the country or more than half the country, wonder 'was that actually the result? Is this the future the country wants?' That's first and foremost, let's be certain, everybody play by the rules." Taylor maintains further, "on the basis of fairness, it has to be the same vote posed in the same way."[22]

In July 2018 the Electoral Commission,[18] Information Commissioner's Office,[19] and the House of Commons Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee issued reports, finding variously criminal offences of overspending by Vote Leave, data offences, and foreign interference by Russia.[23] In August 2018, this led to legal challenges to declare the referendum void for violating common law and United Kingdom constitutional law.[21] In May 2020, the Electoral Commission, which had referred Banks to the National Crime Agency for investigation of these allegations, conceded that he did not break electoral law during the 2016 EU referendum campaign.[24]

The 2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum took place in the United Kingdom and Gibraltar on 23 June 2016.[1][2] Membership of the European Union had been a topic of political debate in the United Kingdom since the country joined the European Communities (then commonly referred to as the "Common Market" by the British people) in 1973. This referendum was conducted very differently from the European Communities membership referendum in 1975; a more localised and regionalised counting procedure was used, and the ballot was overseen by the Electoral Commission, a public body that did not exist at the time of the first vote. This article lists, by voting area for Great Britain and Gibraltar and by parliamentary constituency for Northern Ireland, all the results of the referendum, each ordered into national and regional sections.

Under the provisions of the European Union Referendum Act 2015, there were a total of 382 voting areas across twelve regions, using the same boundaries as used in European Parliamentary elections since 1999, under the provisions of the European Parliamentary Elections Act 2002, with votes counted at local authority level. In England the 326 local government districts were used as the voting areas; these consist of all unitary authorities, all metropolitan boroughs, all shire districts, the London boroughs, the City of London and the Isles of Scilly.[3] The nine regions of England were then also used to count the votes at the regional level, with Gibraltar being regarded as part of South West England. Northern Ireland was a single voting area as well as being a regional count, although local totals by Westminster parliamentary constituency area were announced.[3] In Scotland the 32 Scottish council areas were used as voting areas, and there was a single national count.[3] In Wales the 22 Welsh council areas were used as the voting areas, and there was a single national count.[3]

Verification and counting began as soon as the polls closed on 23 June from 22:00 BST onwards (making it the first UK-wide referendum to be counted overnight) and took nine hours and twenty minutes to complete. The early results showed at different times narrow leads for both Remain and Leave; however, Leave took the lead in the national vote count for the final time at 02:58 BST when Castle Point declared its result. The result of the referendum was forecast by the BBC just before 04:40 BST (around 6 hours 40 minutes after polls closed), with around 308 results declared at the time. The first result announced was Gibraltar, and the last was Cornwall.

On 24 June 2016, the recorded result was that the UK voted to leave the European Union by 51.89% for Leave to 48.11% for Remain, a margin of 3.78%. This corresponded to 17,410,742 votes to leave and 16,141,241 to remain, a margin of 1,269,501 votes.

United Kingdomedit
Of the 382 voting areas in Great Britain and Gibraltar and the 18 Northern Ireland parliamentary constituencies, a total of 270 returned "majority" votes in favour of "Leave the European Union", while 129 returned "majority" votes in favour of "Remain a member of the European Union", including all 32 voting areas in Scotland.

The final result of the referendum for the United Kingdom and Gibraltar was declared at Manchester Town Hall at 0720 BST on Friday 24 June 2016, after all the 382 voting areas and the twelve UK regions had declared their results, by the Chief Counting Officer (CCO) for the referendum, Jenny Watson. In a UK-wide referendum the position of CCO is held by the chair of the Electoral Commission.[4] The following figures are as reported by the Electoral Commission.[5]

"Leave the European Union" secured a majority of 1,269,501 votes (3.78%) over those who had voted in favour of "Remain a member of the European Union". England (except Greater London) and Wales voted to "Leave", while Scotland and Northern Ireland voted to "Remain".

Results from the 30 largest cities in the United Kingdomedit

Out of over 33.5 million valid votes cast across the United Kingdom, over 8.8 million, or just over one quarter, were cast in thirty major cities that each gathered 100,000 votes or more. 16 of those cities voted to Leave, and 14 voted to Remain, or 53% Leave and 47% Remain.

In those 30 cities, votes to Remain outnumbered those to Leave by over 900,000 (about 4.9 million to 4 million or 55.2% to 44.8%), while in the other voting areas, the votes to Leave outnumbered those to Remain by nearly 2.2 million (about 13.5 million to 11.3 million, or 54.4% to 45.6%).

Englandedit

The English local districts were used as the voting areas for the referendum in England; these consist of all unitary authorities, all metropolitan districts, all non-metropolitan districts, the London boroughs, the City of London and the Isles of Scilly.[3]

Unlike the other constituent countries of the United Kingdom there was no centralised national count of the votes in England as counting was done within the nine separate regions. Figures from Gibraltar are included in the South West England region.

While all council counting areas showed a majority to remain, one constituency, Banff and Buchan, voted to leave by an estimated ratio of 54% to 46%.[8][9] Voting to leave the EU was most concentrated around the north coast of Aberdeenshire between the fishing towns of Banff and Peterhead, where there were 23,707 Leave votes to 14,918 Remain votes (61% Leave 39% Remain).[10]

The areas of Whalsay and South Unst in the Shetland Islands and An Taobh Siar and Nis in Na h-Eileanan an Iar (The Western Isles) also voted by a majority for Leave,[11] as did the town of Lossiemouth in Moray.[12][13]

Walesedit
Voting areas of Wales
  Leave
  Remain

The Welsh council areas were used as the voting areas for the referendum throughout Wales.

A total of 650,000 inhabitants born in England live in Wales (21%), with the areas with the highest percentages voting to leave.[14] The majority to leave the EU was 82,000.[14] The map shows council areas comprising ex-heavy industrial places and English-speaking as a common preference as areas where Leave won out. Parts of rural Wales also saw a leave-vote majority (but also Anglesey where Welsh is just as commonly if not more usually spoken). Cardiff, the Plaid Cymru heartland of the two council areas in West Wales, and by wafer-thin margins affluent Monmouthshire and the Vale of Glamorgan were the areas where Remain held sway.

Most evenly divided areasedit

The narrowest margin of victory for any of the 382 voting areas in the United Kingdom was in the Scottish council area of Moray, which voted by just 122 votes or 0.25% margin in favour of Remain.

In England the narrowest margins of victory for Leave were in Watford which voted by just 252 votes or 0.54% margin in favour of Leave, and in Cherwell which voted by just 500 votes or 0.61% margin in favour of Leave. The narrowest margin of victory for Remain was in the London Borough of Bromley, which voted by just 2,364 votes or a 1.30% margin in favour of Remain.

The area with the closest vote to the national result of 51.89% for Leave, was Basingstoke and Deane, where 51.90% of people voted Leave.

Turnout by age groupedit

After the referendum, the annual British Social Attitudes survey questioned the public on their participation. Interviewing was mainly carried out between July and October 2016 and respondents were subdivided into three age groups (18–34, 35–64 and >/=65).[17] The survey revealed that turnout was higher in the older age groups, and was 64%, 80% and 89% respectively. The age disparity had also been a feature of previous elections and referendums. However, compared to the previous referendum in 2011, the young voters' turnout in 2016 had increased sharply by 31%, while turnout by the two older age categories had also increased, but only by 26% and 21%.

Irregularitiesedit
See also: Russian interference in the 2016 Brexit referendum

In July 2018, Vote Leave was found by the Electoral Commission to have broken electoral law, spending over its limit.[18] Connected to this, the Information Commissioner's Office found that data had been unlawfully harvested from UK voters, and issued a notice of intent to fine Facebook £500,000.[19] Also, the House of Commons Culture, Media and Sport Select Committee, released an interim report on "Disinformation and 'fake news'", stating that Russia had engaged in "unconventional warfare" through Twitter and other social media against the United Kingdom, designed to amplify support for a "leave" vote in Brexit. It also found that it could not be satisfied that the largest donor in the Brexit campaign, Arron Banks, used money from UK sources, and found that he might have been financed by the Russian government.[20] This led to litigation to declare the result void.[21] Kyle Taylor of the Fair Vote Project, a campaign group that called for a public inquiry and supported a second referendum, said: "The issue is too big to have half the country or more than half the country, wonder 'was that actually the result? Is this the future the country wants?' That's first and foremost, let's be certain, everybody play by the rules." Taylor maintains further, "on the basis of fairness, it has to be the same vote posed in the same way."[22]

In July 2018 the Electoral Commission,[18] Information Commissioner's Office,[19] and the House of Commons Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee issued reports, finding variously criminal offences of overspending by Vote Leave, data offences, and foreign interference by Russia.[23] In August 2018, this led to legal challenges to declare the referendum void for violating common law and United Kingdom constitutional law.[21] In May 2020, the Electoral Commission, which had referred Banks to the National Crime Agency for investigation of these allegations, conceded that he did not break electoral law during the 2016 EU referendum campaign.[24]

**Bristol** ([/ˈ b r ɪ s t əl/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/f/fb/En-uk-Bristol.ogg/En-uk-Bristol.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:En-uk-Bristol.ogg "File:En-uk-Bristol.ogg")) is a [city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_status_in_the_United_Kingdom "City status in the United Kingdom") and [ceremonial county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceremonial_county "Ceremonial county") in [South West England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_England "South West England"). It is on the [River Avon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Avon,_Bristol "River Avon, Bristol"), and bordered by [Gloucestershire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloucestershire "Gloucestershire") to the north and [Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset "Somerset") to the south, with a short coastline on the [Bristol Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Channel "Bristol Channel") to the west. The county includes most of the [Bristol conurbation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Bristol "Greater Bristol"), but the urban area extends into [South Gloucestershire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Gloucestershire "South Gloucestershire"), [Bath and North East Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath_and_North_East_Somerset "Bath and North East Somerset"), and [North Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Somerset "North Somerset").

The county is almost entirely urbanised and had an estimated population of 494,399 in 2024, making Bristol the most populous city in the region.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-7) For local government purposes the county is a [unitary authority area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_authorities_of_England "Unitary authorities of England") governed by [Bristol City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_City_Council "Bristol City Council"). The council is a member of the [West of England Combined Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_of_England_Combined_Authority "West of England Combined Authority"), which allows it to collaborate with [South Gloucestershire Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Gloucestershire_Council "South Gloucestershire Council") and [Bath and North East Somerset Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath_and_North_East_Somerset_Council "Bath and North East Somerset Council").

[Iron Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age "Iron Age")[hillforts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillfort "Hillfort") and [Roman villas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_villa "Roman villa") were built near the [confluence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confluence "Confluence") of the rivers [Frome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Frome,_Bristol "River Frome, Bristol") and Avon. Bristol received a [royal charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal charter") in 1155, but was [historically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historic_counties_of_England "Historic counties of England") divided between Gloucestershire and Somerset until it became a [county corporate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_corporate "County corporate") in 1373. From the 13th to the 18th centuries, Bristol was among the top three English cities, after London, in tax receipts. A major port, Bristol was a starting place for early voyages of exploration to the New World. At the height of the [Bristol slave trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_slave_trade "Bristol slave trade"), from 1700 to 1807, more than 2,000 slave ships carried an estimated 500,000 people from Africa to slavery in the Americas. The [Port of Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Bristol "Port of Bristol") has since moved from [Bristol Harbour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Harbour "Bristol Harbour") in the city centre to the [Severn Estuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severn_Estuary "Severn Estuary") at [Avonmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avonmouth "Avonmouth") and [Royal Portbury Dock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Portbury_Dock "Royal Portbury Dock").

The city's modern economy is built on the creative media, electronics, and [aerospace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace "Aerospace") industries; the city-centre docks have been redeveloped as cultural and heritage centres. There are a variety of artistic and sporting organisations and venues, including the [Royal West of England Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_West_of_England_Academy "Royal West of England Academy"), the [Arnolfini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnolfini,_Bristol "Arnolfini, Bristol"), [Ashton Gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashton_Gate_Stadium "Ashton Gate Stadium") and the [Memorial Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Ground "Memorial Ground"). The city has two universities: the [University of Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol "University of Bristol") and the [University of the West of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_West_of_England "University of the West of England") (UWE Bristol). It is connected to the world by [Bristol Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Airport "Bristol Airport"); to the rest of [Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain "Great Britain") via [Bristol Temple Meads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Temple_Meads_railway_station "Bristol Temple Meads railway station") and [Bristol Parkway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Parkway_railway_station "Bristol Parkway railway station") mainline rail stations; and by road by both the south-west to [West Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Midlands_(region) "West Midlands (region)")[M5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M5_motorway "M5 motorway") and the London to South Wales [M4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4_motorway "M4 motorway") (which connect to the city centre by the [Portway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portway,_Bristol "Portway, Bristol") and [M32](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M32_motorway "M32 motorway")).

## Toponymy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bristol&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Toponymy")]

The name derives from the [Old English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English "Old English")_Brycgstow_, meaning "assembly place by the bridge" or simply "site of the bridge", presumably in reference to a crossing over the Avon.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-9) The final 'L' is an unetymological addition that first appears in the 12th century, which may be due to the unique "Terminal L" found in the [Bristol dialect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_in_Bristol#Dialect "Culture in Bristol"). An older form of the name survives as the surname [Bristow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristow_(surname) "Bristow (surname)"), which derives from the city.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-10)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bristol&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

Main articles: [History of Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Bristol "History of Bristol") and [Timeline of Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Bristol "Timeline of Bristol")

[Archaeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeological "Archaeological") finds, including flint tools believed to be between 300,000 and 126,000 years old made with the [Levallois technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levallois_technique "Levallois technique"), indicate the presence of [Neanderthals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neanderthal "Neanderthal") in the [Shirehampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirehampton "Shirehampton") and [St Annes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brislington_West_(ward) "Brislington West (ward)") areas of Bristol during the [Middle Palaeolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Palaeolithic "Middle Palaeolithic").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-11)[Iron Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age "Iron Age")[hill forts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hill_fort "Hill fort") near the city are at [Leigh Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leigh_Woods "Leigh Woods") and [Clifton Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifton_Down "Clifton Down"), on the side of the [Avon Gorge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avon_Gorge "Avon Gorge"), and on [Kings Weston Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kings_Weston_Hill "Kings Weston Hill") near [Henbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henbury,_Bristol "Henbury, Bristol").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-12) A [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Britain "Roman Britain") port, _Portus Abonae_ (Avonport) – abbreviated to _Abona_ in the [Antonine Itinerary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonine_Itinerary "Antonine Itinerary"),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-13) existed at what is now [Sea Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Mills,_Bristol "Sea Mills, Bristol") (connected to [Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath,_Somerset "Bath, Somerset") and [Gloucester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloucester "Gloucester") by [Roman roads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_road "Roman road")); another settlement was at the present-day [Inns Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filwood_(ward)#Inns_Court "Filwood (ward)"). Isolated [Roman villas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_villa "Roman villa") and small [forts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castra "Castra") and settlements were also scattered throughout the area.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-14)

### Middle Ages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bristol&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Middle Ages")]

Bristol was founded by 1000; by about 1020, it was a trading centre with a [mint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mint_(coin) "Mint (coin)") producing silver pennies bearing its name.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTELobelCarus-Wilson19752%E2%80%933-15) By 1067, Brycgstow was a well-fortified _[burh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burh "Burh")_, and that year the townsmen beat back a raiding party from Ireland led by three of [Harold Godwinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Godwinson "Harold Godwinson")'s sons.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTELobelCarus-Wilson19752%E2%80%933-15) Under [Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normans "Normans") rule, the town had one of the strongest [castles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Castle "Bristol Castle") in [southern England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_England "Southern England").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-16) Bristol was the place of exile for [Diarmait Mac Murchada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diarmait_Mac_Murchada "Diarmait Mac Murchada"), the Irish [king of Leinster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Leinster "King of Leinster"), after being overthrown. The Bristol merchants subsequently played a prominent role in funding [Richard Strongbow de Clare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Strongbow_de_Clare "Richard Strongbow de Clare") and the [Norman invasion of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_invasion_of_Ireland "Norman invasion of Ireland").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-17)

[![Image 14: Fifteenth-century pictorial map of Bristol, radiating from the town centre](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/d/d0/Robert_Ricart%27s_map_of_Bristol.png/250px-Robert_Ricart%27s_map_of_Bristol.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Robert_Ricart's_map_of_Bristol.png)

[Robert Ricart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Maire_of_Bristowe_is_Kalendar "The Maire of Bristowe is Kalendar")'s map of Bristol, drawn when he became common clerk of the town in 1478. At the centre, it shows the [High Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_High_Cross "Bristol High Cross"), moved in 1764 to the [Stourhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stourhead "Stourhead") estate.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-18)

The port developed in the 11th century around the confluence of the [Rivers Frome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Frome,_Bristol "River Frome, Bristol") and [Avon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Avon_(Bristol) "River Avon (Bristol)"), adjacent to [Bristol Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Bridge "Bristol Bridge") just outside the town walls.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrace197613%E2%80%9315-19) By the 12th century, there was an important [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_England "History of the Jews in England") community in Bristol which survived through to the late 13th century when all Jews were [expelled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Expulsion "Edict of Expulsion") from England.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-20) The stone bridge built in 1247 was replaced by the current bridge during the 1760s.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-21) The town incorporated neighbouring suburbs and became a [county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_corporate "County corporate") in 1373,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTELiddy200513-22) the first town in England to be given this status.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTERayfield198517%E2%80%9323-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-25) During this period, Bristol became a shipbuilding and manufacturing centre.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarus-Wilson1933183%E2%80%93246-26) By the 14th century, Bristol, [York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York "York") and [Norwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich "Norwich") were England's largest [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval "Medieval") towns after London.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-27) One-third to one-half of the population died in the [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death") of 1348–49,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCulloch1839398%E2%80%93399-28) which checked population growth, and its population remained between 10,000 and 12,000 for most of the 15th and 16th centuries.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-29)

### 15th and 16th centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bristol&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 15th and 16th centuries")]

[![Image 15: A stone-built Victorian Gothic building with two square towers and a central arched entrance underneath a circular ornate window. A Victorian street lamp stands in front of the building and on the right part of a leafless tree, with blue skies behind.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/Bristol.cathedral.west.front.arp.jpg/250px-Bristol.cathedral.west.front.arp.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bristol.cathedral.west.front.arp.jpg)

West front of [Bristol Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Cathedral "Bristol Cathedral")

During the 15th century, Bristol was the second most important port in the country, trading with Ireland,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-30) Iceland[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarus-Wilson1933155%E2%80%93182-31) and [Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascony "Gascony").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarus-Wilson1933183%E2%80%93246-26) It was the starting point for many voyages, including [Robert Sturmy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Sturmy "Robert Sturmy")'s (1457–58) unsuccessful attempt to break the Italian [monopoly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monopoly "Monopoly") of Eastern Mediterranean trade.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJenks20061-32) New exploration voyages were launched by Venetian [John Cabot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cabot "John Cabot"), who in 1497 made landfall in North America.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJonesCondon2016-33) A 1499 voyage, led by merchant [William Weston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Weston_(explorer) "William Weston (explorer)") of Bristol, was the first expedition commanded by an Englishman to [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-34) During the first decade of the 16th century, Bristol's merchants undertook a series of exploration voyages to North America and even founded a commercial organisation, 'The Company Adventurers to the New Found Land', to assist their endeavours.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJonesCondon201657%E2%80%9370-35) However, they seem to have lost interest in North America after 1509, having incurred great expenses and made little profit.

During the 16th century, Bristol merchants concentrated on developing trade with Spain and its American colonies.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTEConnell-Smith195410-36) This included the [smuggling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smuggling "Smuggling") of prohibited goods, such as food and guns, to Iberia[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-37) during the [Anglo-Spanish War (1585–1604)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Spanish_War_(1585%E2%80%931604) "Anglo-Spanish War (1585–1604)").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-38) Bristol's illicit trade grew enormously after 1558, becoming integral to its economy.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones2012-39)

The original [Diocese of Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_of_Bristol "Diocese of Bristol") was founded in 1542,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-40) when the former [Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbey "Abbey") of [St. Augustine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_of_Canterbury "Augustine of Canterbury") (founded by [Robert Fitzharding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Fitzharding "Robert Fitzharding") four hundred years earlier)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBettey19961%E2%80%935-41) became [Bristol Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Cathedral "Bristol Cathedral"). Bristol also gained [city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_status_in_the_United_Kingdom "City status in the United Kingdom") status that year.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-42)

### 17th and 18th centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bristol&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 17th and 18th centuries")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Charles_E._Flower%2C_The_Old_Dutch_House%2C_Bristol.jpg/250px-Charles_E._Flower%2C_The_Old_Dutch_House%2C_Bristol.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Charles_E._Flower,_The_Old_Dutch_House,_Bristol.jpg)

The 17th-century Old Dutch House, High Street, Bristol, before destruction in the Blitz, 1940

In the 1640s, during the [English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War"), [the city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_in_the_English_Civil_War "Bristol in the English Civil War") was occupied by [Royalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier"), who built the [Royal Fort House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Fort_House "Royal Fort House") on the site of an earlier [Parliamentarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") stronghold.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-43)

Fishermen from Bristol, who had fished the [Grand Banks of Newfoundland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Banks_of_Newfoundland "Grand Banks of Newfoundland") since the 16th century,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-44) began settling Newfoundland permanently in larger numbers during the 17th century, establishing colonies at [Bristol's Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol's_Hope "Bristol's Hope") and [Cuper's Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuper's_Cove "Cuper's Cove"). Growth of the city and trade came with the rise of England's [American colonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_colonization_of_the_Americas "European colonization of the Americas") in the 17th century. Bristol's location on the west side of Great Britain gave its ships an advantage in sailing to and from the New World, and the city's merchants made the most of it, with the city becoming one of the two leading outports in all of England by the middle of the 18th century.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-45) Bristol was the slave capital of England: In 1755, it had the largest number of slave traders in the country with 237, as against London's 147.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-46) It was a major supplier of slaves to [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina") before 1750.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-47)
