Below a street scene showing pedestrians and a horse-drawn carriage outside a large ornate building with a colonnade and arched windows above. A grand staircase with two figures ascending and other figures on a balcony. A caption reading "Exterior, Colston Hall" and Staircase, Colston Hall". Below, two street scenes and a view of a large stone building with flying buttresses and a square tower, with the caption "Bristol cathedral". At the bottom views of a church interior, a cloister with a man mowing grass and archways with two men in conversation.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Bristol_1873.png/250px-Bristol_1873.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bristol_1873.png)

An 1873 engraving showing [Colston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Colston "Edward Colston") Hall, the port and cathedral of Bristol

The 18th century saw an expansion of Bristol's population (45,000 in 1750)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-48) and its role in the [Atlantic trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_slave_trade "Atlantic slave trade") in Africans taken for [slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery "Slavery") to the Americas. Bristol and later [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool "Liverpool") became centres of the [Triangular Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangular_Trade "Triangular Trade").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-49) Manufactured goods were shipped to West Africa and exchanged for Africans; the enslaved captives were transported across the Atlantic to the Americas in the [Middle Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Passage "Middle Passage") under brutal conditions.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-nmm-50) Plantation goods such as sugar, tobacco, rum, rice, cotton and a few slaves (sold to the aristocracy as house servants) returned across the Atlantic to England.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-nmm-50) Some household slaves were baptised in the hope this would lead them to be freed. The [Somersett Case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somersett_Case "Somersett Case") of 1772 clarified that slavery was illegal in England.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-51) At the height of the [Bristol slave trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_slave_trade "Bristol slave trade") from 1700 to 1807, more than 2,000 slave ships carried a conservatively estimated 500,000 people from Africa to slavery in the Americas.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-52)

In 1739, [John Wesley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wesley "John Wesley") founded the first [Methodist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodist "Methodist") chapel, the [New Room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Room "New Room"), in Bristol.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-53) Wesley, along with his brother [Charles Wesley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Wesley "Charles Wesley") and [George Whitefield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Whitefield "George Whitefield"), preached to large congregations in Bristol and the neighbouring village of [Kingswood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingswood,_South_Gloucestershire "Kingswood, South Gloucestershire"), often in the open air.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-55)

Wesley published a pamphlet on slavery, titled _Thoughts Upon Slavery,_ in 1774[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-56) and the [Society of Friends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Friends "Society of Friends") began lobbying against slavery in Bristol in 1783. The city's scions remained nonetheless strongly anti-abolitionist. [Thomas Clarkson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Clarkson "Thomas Clarkson") came to Bristol to study the slave trade and gained access to the [Society of Merchant Venturers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Merchant_Venturers "Society of Merchant Venturers") records.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-BRS#1-57) One of his contacts was the owner of the [Seven Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Stars,_Bristol "Seven Stars, Bristol")[public house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_house "Public house"), who boarded sailors Clarkson sought to meet. Through these sailors he was able to observe how slaver captains and first mates "plied and stupefied seamen with drink" to sign them up.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-BRS#1-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-58) Other informants included ship surgeons and seamen seeking redress. When [William Wilberforce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wilberforce "William Wilberforce") began his parliamentary abolition campaign on 12 May 1788, he recalled the history of the [Irish slave trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_slave_trade "Irish slave trade") from Bristol, which he provocatively claimed continued into the reign of [Henry VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VII_of_England "Henry VII of England").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-BRS#1-57)[Hannah More](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannah_More "Hannah More"), originally from Bristol, and a good friend of both Wilberforce and Clarkson, published "Slavery, A Poem" in 1788, just as Wilberforce began his parliamentary campaign.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-59) His major speech on 2 April 1792 likewise described the Bristol slave trade specifically, and led to the arrest, trial and subsequent acquittal of a local slaver captain named Kimber.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-BRS#1-57)

### 19th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bristol&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 19th century")]

The city was associated with Victorian engineer [Isambard Kingdom Brunel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isambard_Kingdom_Brunel "Isambard Kingdom Brunel"), who designed the [Great Western Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Western_Railway "Great Western Railway") between Bristol and [London Paddington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Paddington "London Paddington"), two pioneering Bristol-built oceangoing [steamships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steamboat "Steamboat") ([SS _Great Britain_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Great_Britain "SS Great Britain") and [SS _Great Western_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Great_Western "SS Great Western")), and the [Clifton Suspension Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifton_Suspension_Bridge "Clifton Suspension Bridge"). The new railway replaced the [Kennet and Avon Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennet_and_Avon_Canal "Kennet and Avon Canal"), which had fully opened in 1810, as the main route for the transport of goods between Bristol and London.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClew197079%E2%80%9380-60) Competition from Liverpool (beginning around 1760), disruptions of maritime commerce due to war with France (1793) and the abolition of the slave trade (1807) contributed to Bristol's failure to keep pace with the newer manufacturing centres of [Northern England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_England "Northern England") and the [West Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Midlands_(region) "West Midlands (region)"). The tidal Avon Gorge, which had secured the port during the Middle Ages, had become a liability. An 1804–09 plan to improve the city's port with a [floating harbour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Harbour "Bristol Harbour") designed by [William Jessop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Jessop "William Jessop") was a costly error, requiring high harbour fees.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuchananCossons196932%E2%80%9333-61)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Bristol_Harbour_%28St_Stephen%27s_Church%2C_St_Augustine_the_Less_Church%2C_Bristol_Cathedral%29%2C_BRO_Picbox-7-PBA-22%2C_1250x1250.jpg/250px-Bristol_Harbour_%28St_Stephen%27s_Church%2C_St_Augustine_the_Less_Church%2C_Bristol_Cathedral%29%2C_BRO_Picbox-7-PBA-22%2C_1250x1250.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bristol_Harbour_(St_Stephen's_Church,_St_Augustine_the_Less_Church,_Bristol_Cathedral),_BRO_Picbox-7-PBA-22,_1250x1250.jpg)

Black-and-white etching showing the towers of [St Stephen's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Stephen's_Church,_Bristol "St Stephen's Church, Bristol"), [St Augustine the Less Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Augustine_the_Less_Church,_Bristol "St Augustine the Less Church, Bristol") and [Bristol Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Cathedral "Bristol Cathedral"), published c.1850

During the 19th century, [Samuel Plimsoll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Plimsoll "Samuel Plimsoll"), known as "the sailor's friend", campaigned to make the seas safer; shocked by overloaded vessels, he successfully fought for a compulsory [load line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Load_line_(vessel) "Load line (vessel)") on ships.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-62)

By 1867, ships were getting larger and the meanders in the river Avon prevented boats over 300 ft (90 m) from reaching the harbour, resulting in falling trade.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoules2006194%E2%80%93195-63) The port facilities were migrating downstream to [Avonmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avonmouth "Avonmouth") and new industrial complexes were founded there.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuchananCossons1969224%E2%80%93225-64) Some of the traditional industries including copper and brass manufacture went into decline,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-65) but the import and processing of [tobacco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobacco "Tobacco") flourished with the expansion of the [W.D. & H.O. Wills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W.D._&_H.O._Wills "W.D. & H.O. Wills") business.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-66)

Supported by new industry and growing commerce, Bristol's population (66,000 in 1801), quintupled during the 19th century,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-67) resulting in the creation of new suburbs such as [Clifton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifton,_Bristol "Clifton, Bristol") and [Cotham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotham,_Bristol "Cotham, Bristol"). These provide architectural examples from the Georgian to the Regency style, with many fine terraces and villas facing the road, and at right angles to it. In the early 19th century, the romantic [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval "Medieval")[gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_revival "Gothic revival") style appeared, partially as a reaction against the [symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry "Symmetry") of [Palladianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palladianism "Palladianism"), and can be seen in buildings such as the [Bristol City Museum and Art Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_City_Museum_and_Art_Gallery "Bristol City Museum and Art Gallery"),[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-68) the [Royal West of England Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_West_of_England_Academy "Royal West of England Academy"),[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-69) and [The Victoria Rooms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Victoria_Rooms "The Victoria Rooms").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-Victoria_Rooms-70)[Riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_riots "Bristol riots") broke out in 1793[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunt1818-71) and 1831; the first over the renewal of [tolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toll_road "Toll road") on Bristol Bridge, and the second against the rejection of the second [Reform Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Act_1832 "Reform Act 1832") by the [House of Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lords "House of Lords").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-72) The population by 1841 had reached 140,158.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-73)

The Diocese of Bristol had undergone several boundary changes by 1897 when it was "reconstituted" into the configuration which has lasted into the 21st century.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-74)

### 20th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bristol&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 20th century")]

[![Image 19: An old ordnance survey map of Bristol, showing roads, railways, rivers and contours.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Bristol_map_1946.jpg/250px-Bristol_map_1946.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bristol_map_1946.jpg)

A 1946 map of Bristol

From a population of about 330,000 in 1901, Bristol grew steadily during the 20th century, peaking at 428,089 in 1971.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-visiontime-75) Its Avonmouth docklands were enlarged during the early 1900s by the Royal Edward Dock.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-76) Another new dock, the [Royal Portbury Dock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Portbury_Dock "Royal Portbury Dock"), opened across the river from Avonmouth during the 1970s.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-77) As air travel grew in the first half of the century, aircraft manufacturers built factories.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-78) The unsuccessful [Bristol International Exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_International_Exhibition "Bristol International Exhibition") was held on Ashton Meadows in the [Bower Ashton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bower_Ashton "Bower Ashton") area in 1914.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-79) After the premature closure of the exhibition the site was used, until 1919, as [barracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barracks "Barracks") for the [Gloucestershire Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloucestershire_Regiment "Gloucestershire Regiment") during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurlton201460%E2%80%9390-81)

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/St_Mary_le_Port_Church%2C_Bristol%2C_BRO_Picbox-3-Blitz-4a%2C_1250x1250.jpg/250px-St_Mary_le_Port_Church%2C_Bristol%2C_BRO_Picbox-3-Blitz-4a%2C_1250x1250.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_Mary_le_Port_Church,_Bristol,_BRO_Picbox-3-Blitz-4a,_1250x1250.jpg)

St Mary le Port Church, destroyed on 24 November 1940

[Bristol was heavily damaged by Luftwaffe raids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Blitz "Bristol Blitz") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"); about 1,300 people living or working in the city were killed, and nearly 100,000 buildings were damaged, at least 3,000 beyond repair.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-82)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-83) The original central shopping area, near the bridge and castle, [is now a park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_Park,_Bristol "Castle Park, Bristol") containing two bombed churches and fragments of the castle. A third bomb-damaged church nearby, [St Nicholas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Nicholas_Church,_Bristol "St Nicholas Church, Bristol"), was restored and, after a period as a museum, has now re-opened as a church.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-84) It houses a 1756 [William Hogarth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hogarth "William Hogarth")[triptych](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triptych "Triptych") painted for the high altar of [St Mary Redcliffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Mary_Redcliffe "St Mary Redcliffe"). The church also has statues of [King Edward I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Edward_I "King Edward I") (moved from [Arno's Court Triumphal Arch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arno's_Court_Triumphal_Arch "Arno's Court Triumphal Arch")) and [King Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Edward_III "King Edward III") (taken from Lawfords' Gate in the city walls when they were demolished about 1760), and 13th-century statues of [Robert, 1st Earl of Gloucester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert,_1st_Earl_of_Gloucester "Robert, 1st Earl of Gloucester") (builder of [Bristol Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Castle "Bristol Castle"))[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-85) and [Geoffrey de Montbray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_de_Montbray "Geoffrey de Montbray") (who built the city's walls) from Bristol's [Newgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newgate,_Bristol "Newgate, Bristol").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-86)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Ambrose_Rd%2C_Bristol.jpg/250px-Ambrose_Rd%2C_Bristol.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ambrose_Rd,_Bristol.jpg)

Ambrose Road, in the Cliftonwood neighbourhood

The rebuilding of [Bristol city centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_city_centre "Bristol city centre") was characterised by 1960s and 1970s [skyscrapers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skyscraper "Skyscraper"), [mid-century modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-century_modern "Mid-century modern") architecture and [road building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Century_Road_Schemes_in_Bristol "20th Century Road Schemes in Bristol"). Beginning in the 1980s some [main roads were closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Century_Road_Schemes_in_Bristol#Queen_Square,_Redcliffe_Way_and_The_Centre "20th Century Road Schemes in Bristol"), the [Georgian-era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian_era "Georgian era")[Queen Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Square,_Bristol "Queen Square, Bristol") and [Portland Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_Square,_Bristol "Portland Square, Bristol") were restored, the [Broadmead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadmead "Broadmead") shopping area regenerated, and one of the city centre's tallest mid-century towers was demolished.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-87) Bristol's road infrastructure changed dramatically during the 1960s and 1970s with the development of the [M4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4_motorway "M4 motorway") and [M5 motorways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M5_motorway "M5 motorway"), which meet at the [Almondsbury Interchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almondsbury_Interchange "Almondsbury Interchange") just north of the city and link Bristol with London (M4 eastbound), [Swansea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swansea "Swansea") (M4 westbound across the [Severn Estuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severn_Estuary "Severn Estuary")), [Exeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exeter "Exeter") (M5 southbound) and [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham") (M5 northbound).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Bristol was bombed twice by the [IRA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_IRA "Provisional IRA"), in [1974](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Bristol_bombing "1974 Bristol bombing") and again in [1978](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_terrorist_incidents_in_Great_Britain#1970s "List of terrorist incidents in Great Britain").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-88)

The 20th-century relocation of the docks to [Avonmouth Docks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avonmouth_Docks "Avonmouth Docks") and [Royal Portbury Dock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Portbury_Dock "Royal Portbury Dock"), 7 mi (11 km) downstream from the city centre, has allowed the redevelopment of the old dock area (the Floating Harbour).[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-89) Although the docks' existence was once in jeopardy (since the area was seen as a derelict industrial site), the inaugural 1996 [International Festival of the Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Festival_of_the_Sea,_1996 "International Festival of the Sea, 1996") held in and around the docks affirmed the area as a leisure asset of the city.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-90)

On 7 June 2020 a [Statue of Edward Colston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_Edward_Colston "Statue of Edward Colston") was pulled down from its city centre plinth by protestors and pushed into the harbour.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-91) The statue was recovered on 11 June and has become a museum exhibit.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-92) The action followed more than a decade of debate over the statue and the wording of its plaque, which commemorated Colston's philanthropic work in the city while making no reference to his role in the [Royal African Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_African_Company "Royal African Company") and the [Bristol Slave Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Slave_Trade "Bristol Slave Trade").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-93)

Between 2012 and 2024, the council was led by a directly elected mayor, the [Mayor of Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Bristol "Mayor of Bristol"). The post was abolished following a 2022 referendum, in which voters chose to replace it with a council committee system.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-96)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-97)

The [lord mayor of Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mayors_of_Bristol "List of mayors of Bristol") is a figurehead elected each May by the city council. The lord mayor (2026) is Henry Michallat.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-bbc_lord_mayor_2026-3)

In the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom"), Bristol is represented by five constituencies, [East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_East_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Bristol East (UK Parliament constituency)"), [North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_North_East_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Bristol North East (UK Parliament constituency)"), [North West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_North_West_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Bristol North West (UK Parliament constituency)"), [South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_South_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Bristol South (UK Parliament constituency)"), and [Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Central_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Bristol Central (UK Parliament constituency)").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-98)

The city has a tradition of political activism. [Edmund Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Burke "Edmund Burke"), MP for the [Bristol constituency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Bristol (UK Parliament constituency)") for six years beginning in 1774, insisted that he was a Member of Parliament first and a representative of his constituents' interests second.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-99)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-100) Women's-rights advocate [Emmeline Pethick-Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmeline_Pethick-Lawrence "Emmeline Pethick-Lawrence") (1867–1954) was born in Bristol,[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-101) and the [left-winger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-wing_politics "Left-wing politics")[Tony Benn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Benn "Tony Benn") served as MP for [Bristol South East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_South_East "Bristol South East") from 1950 to 1960 and again from 1963 to 1983.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-102) In 1963 the [Bristol Bus Boycott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Bus_Boycott "Bristol Bus Boycott"), following the [Bristol Omnibus Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Omnibus_Company "Bristol Omnibus Company")'s refusal to hire black drivers and conductors, drove the passage of the UK's 1965 [Race Relations Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_Relations_Act_1965 "Race Relations Act 1965").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-103) The [1980 St Pauls riot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_St_Pauls_riot "1980 St Pauls riot") protested against racism and police harassment and showed mounting dissatisfaction with the socioeconomic circumstances of the city's Afro-Caribbean residents. Local support of [fair trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_trade "Fair trade") was recognised in 2005, when Bristol became a [fairtrade zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairtrade_zone "Fairtrade zone").[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-104)

Bristol is both a city and a county, since [King Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Edward_III "King Edward III") granted it a county charter in 1373.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTELiddy200513-22) The county was expanded in 1835 to include suburbs such as [Clifton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifton,_Bristol "Clifton, Bristol"), and it was named a [county borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_borough "County borough") in 1889 when that designation was introduced.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTERayfield198517%E2%80%9323-24)

### Former county of Avon

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bristol&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Former county of Avon")]

Main article: [Avon (county)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avon_(county) "Avon (county)")

On 1 April 1974, Bristol became a local government district of the administrative county of [Avon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avon_(county) "Avon (county)").[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-105) On 1 April 1996, Avon was abolished and Bristol became a [unitary authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_authority "Unitary authority").[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-106)

The former Avon area, called [Greater Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Bristol "Greater Bristol") by the Government Office of the South West (now abolished) and others,[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-107) refers to the city and the three neighbouring local authorities‍—‌[Bath and North East Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath_and_North_East_Somerset "Bath and North East Somerset"), [North Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Somerset "North Somerset") and [South Gloucestershire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Gloucestershire "South Gloucestershire") previously in Avon.

The [North Fringe of Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Fringe_of_Bristol "North Fringe of Bristol"), a developed area between the Bristol city boundary and the M4, M5 and M32 motorways (now in South Gloucestershire) was so named as part of a 1987 [plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_plan "Local plan") prepared by the [Northavon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northavon "Northavon") District Council of Avon county.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-108)

### West of England Combined Authority

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bristol&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: West of England Combined Authority")]

Main article: [West of England Combined Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_of_England_Combined_Authority "West of England Combined Authority")

The [West of England Combined Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_of_England_Combined_Authority "West of England Combined Authority") was created on 9 February 2017.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-SI_2017_No_126-109) Covering Bristol and the rest of the old Avon county with the exception of North Somerset, the new [combined authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combined_authority "Combined authority") has responsibility for regional planning, roads, and local transport, and to a lesser extent, education and business investment. The authority is led by the [Mayor of the West of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_the_West_of_England "Mayor of the West of England"), [Helen Godwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Godwin "Helen Godwin").

Bristol's boundaries can be defined in several ways, including those of the city itself, the developed area, or [Greater Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Bristol "Greater Bristol").

The [city council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Bristol "Politics of Bristol") boundary is the narrowest definition of the city itself. However, it unusually includes a large, roughly rectangular section of the western [Severn Estuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severn_Estuary "Severn Estuary") ending at (but not including) the islands of [Flat Holm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flat_Holm "Flat Holm") (in [Cardiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff "Cardiff"), Wales) and [Steep Holm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steep_Holm "Steep Holm").[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-110) This "seaward extension" can be traced back to the original boundary of the County of Bristol laid out in the charter[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-111) granted to the city by [Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III "Edward III") in 1373.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-112)

The [Office for National Statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_for_National_Statistics "Office for National Statistics") (ONS) has defined a [Bristol Urban Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Urban_Area "Bristol Urban Area"), which includes developed areas adjoining Bristol but outside the city-council boundary, such as [Kingswood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingswood,_South_Gloucestershire "Kingswood, South Gloucestershire"), [Mangotsfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangotsfield "Mangotsfield"), [Stoke Gifford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoke_Gifford "Stoke Gifford"), [Winterbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winterbourne,_Gloucestershire "Winterbourne, Gloucestershire"), [Almondsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almondsbury "Almondsbury"), [Easton in Gordano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easton_in_Gordano "Easton in Gordano"), [Whitchurch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitchurch,_Bristol "Whitchurch, Bristol") village, [Filton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filton "Filton"), [Patchway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patchway "Patchway") and [Bradley Stoke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradley_Stoke "Bradley Stoke"), but excludes undeveloped areas within that boundary.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-113)

### Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bristol&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Geography")]

Bristol lies within a [limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone "Limestone") area running from the [Mendip Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendip_Hills "Mendip Hills") in the south to the [Cotswolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotswolds "Cotswolds") in the northeast.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-114) The rivers Avon and Frome cut through the limestone to the underlying clay, creating Bristol's characteristically hilly landscape. The Avon flows from Bath in the east, through [flood plains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flood_plains "Flood plains") and areas which were marshes before the city's growth. To the west, the Avon cuts through the limestone to form the Avon Gorge, formed largely by glacial meltwater after the [last ice age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternary_glaciation "Quaternary glaciation").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-10.1144/GSL-115)

The gorge, which helped protect Bristol Harbour, has been quarried for stone to build the city, and its surrounding land has been protected from development as [The Downs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Downs,_Bristol "The Downs, Bristol") and Leigh Woods. The Avon [estuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estuary "Estuary") and the gorge form the county boundary with [North Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Somerset "North Somerset"), and the river flows into the [Severn Estuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severn_Estuary "Severn Estuary") at [Avonmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avonmouth "Avonmouth"). A smaller gorge, cut by the [Hazel Brook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazel_Brook "Hazel Brook") which flows into the [River Trym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Trym "River Trym"), crosses the [Blaise Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blaise_Castle "Blaise Castle") estate in northern Bristol.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-10.1144/GSL-115)

Bristol is sometimes described, by its inhabitants, as being built on seven hills, like Rome. From 18th-century guidebooks, these seven hills were known as simply Bristol (the Old Town), Castle Hill, College Green, Kingsdown, St Michael's Hill, [Brandon Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon_Hill,_Bristol "Brandon Hill, Bristol") and Redcliffe Hill.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-116) Other local hills include Red Lion Hill, [Barton Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barton_Hill,_Bristol "Barton Hill, Bristol"), [Lawrence Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Hill,_Bristol "Lawrence Hill, Bristol"), Black Boy Hill, Constitution Hill, [Staple Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staple_Hill,_Gloucestershire "Staple Hill, Gloucestershire"), [Windmill Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windmill_Hill,_Bristol "Windmill Hill, Bristol"), Malborough Hill, Nine Tree Hill, Talbot, Brook Hill and Granby Hill.

Bristol is 106 mi (171 km) west of London, 77 mi (124 km) south-southwest of [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham") and 26 mi (42 km) east of the Welsh capital [Cardiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff "Cardiff"). Areas adjoining the city fall within a loosely defined area known as [Greater Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Bristol "Greater Bristol"). [Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath,_Somerset "Bath, Somerset") is located 11 mi (18 km) southeast of the city centre, [Weston-super-Mare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weston-super-Mare "Weston-super-Mare") is 18 mi (29 km) to the southwest and the Welsh city of [Newport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport,_Wales "Newport, Wales") is 19 mi (31 km) to the north west.

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bristol&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Climate")]

The climate is [oceanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate") ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"): _Cfb)_, milder than most places in England and United Kingdom.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-117)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-118) Located in southern England, Bristol is one of the warmest cities in the UK with a mean annual temperature of approximately 11°C (52°F).[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-119)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-120) It is among the sunniest, with more than 1,600 hours of sunshine per year.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-121) Although the city is partially sheltered by the Mendip Hills, it is exposed to the Severn Estuary and the [Bristol Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Channel "Bristol Channel"). Rain is fairly evenly distributed throughout the year, with autumn and winter the wetter seasons. The Atlantic Ocean influences Bristol's weather, keeping its average temperature above freezing throughout the year, but winter frosts are frequent and snow occasionally falls from early November to late April. Summers are warm and drier, with variable sunshine, rain and clouds, and spring weather is unsettled.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-122)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-123)

The weather stations nearest Bristol for which long-term climate data are available are Long Ashton (about 5 mi (8 km) south west of the city centre) and Bristol Weather Station, in the city centre. Data collection at these locations ended in 2002 and 2001, respectively, and following the closure of Filton Airfield, Almondsbury is the nearest weather station to the city.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-MO_stations_2024-124) Temperatures at Long Ashton from 1959 to 2002 ranged from 33.5°C (92.3°F) in July 1976[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-125) to −14.4°C (6.1°F) in January 1982.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-126) Monthly high temperatures since 2002 at Filton exceeding those recorded at Long Ashton include 25.7°C (78.3°F) in April 2003,[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-127)34.5°C (94.1°F) in July 2006[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-128) and 26.8°C (80.2°F) in October 2011.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-129) The lowest recent temperature at Filton was −10.1°C (13.8°F) in December 2010.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-130) Although large cities in general experience an [urban heat island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_heat_island "Urban heat island") effect, with warmer temperatures than their surrounding rural areas, this phenomenon is minimal in Bristol.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-131)

### Environment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bristol&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Environment")]

Main article: [Environment in Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environment_in_Bristol "Environment in Bristol")

Bristol was ranked as Britain's most sustainable city (based on its environmental performance, quality of life, [future-proofing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future-proofing "Future-proofing") and approaches to climate change, recycling and biodiversity), topping environmental charity [Forum for the Future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forum_for_the_Future "Forum for the Future")'s 2008 [Sustainable Cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_city "Sustainable city") Index.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-136)[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-137) Local initiatives include [Sustrans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustrans "Sustrans") (creators of the [National Cycle Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Cycle_Network "National Cycle Network"), founded as Cyclebag in 1977)[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-FOOTNOTECottonGrimshaw2002-138) and Resourcesaver, a non-profit business established in 1988 by Avon Friends of the Earth.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-139) The city regularly features in the annual _[Sunday Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday\_Times "Sunday Times")_ lists of best places in Britain in which to live, topping the list of cities in 2014 and 2017.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-140)[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-141) The city received the 2015 [European Green Capital Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Green_Capital_Award "European Green Capital Award"), becoming the first UK city to receive this award.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-142)

In 2019 Bristol City Council voted in favour of banning all privately owned [diesel cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diesel_engine "Diesel engine") from the city centre.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-bbc._Bris-143) Since then, the plans have been revised in favour of a [clean air zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clean_air_zone "Clean air zone") whereby older and more polluting vehicles will be charged to drive through the city centre. The Clean Air Zone came into effect in November 2022.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol#cite_note-144)

### Green belt

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bristol&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Green belt")]

Main article: [Avon Green Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avon_Green_Belt "Avon Green Belt")

The city has a green belt mainly along its southern fringes, taking in small areas within the [Ashton Court Estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashton_Court "Ashton Court"), South Bristol crematorium and cemetery, High Ridge common and Whitchurch, with a further area around Frenchay Farm. The belt extends outside the city boundaries into surrounding counties and districts, for several miles in places, to afford protection from [urban sprawl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_sprawl "Urban sprawl") to surrounding villages and towns.

The **University of Bristol** is a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in Bristol, England. It received its [royal charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal charter") in 1909,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-Bristolwebsite-8) although it can trace its roots to [University College, Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_College,_Bristol "University College, Bristol"), established in 1876.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-BristolUniversityHistory-9)[Bristol Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Medical_School "Bristol Medical School"), founded in 1833, was merged with the university college in 1893, and later became the university's school of medicine.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-10)

The university is organised into three academic faculties composed of multiple schools and departments running over 200 undergraduate courses, largely in the [Tyndall's Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyndall's_Park "Tyndall's Park") area of the city.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-11) It had a total income of £1.16 billion in 2024–25, of which £342.1 million was from research grants and contracts, with an expenditure of £1.09 billion.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-Bristol_Financial_Statement_24/25-2) The University of Bristol's alumni and faculty include 13 Nobel laureates.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-12)

Bristol is a member of the Russell Group of research-intensive British universities,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-13) the European-wide [Coimbra Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coimbra_Group "Coimbra Group")[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-CoimbraGroup-14) and the [Worldwide Universities Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worldwide_Universities_Network "Worldwide Universities Network").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-WUN-15)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Bristol&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Main article: [History of the University of Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_University_of_Bristol "History of the University of Bristol")

### Foundation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Bristol&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Foundation")]

The university was the successor to [University College Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_College_Bristol "University College Bristol"), founded in 1876. The college was open from the start to both men and women, and opened with 99 day students (30 men and 69 women) and 243 evening students (143 men and 95 women).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-BristolUniversityHistory-9)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-16) The university college was the first such institution in the country to [admit women on the same basis as men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-sex_education "Mixed-sex education").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_][The botanic garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol_Botanic_Garden "University of Bristol Botanic Garden") was established in 1882, originally adjacent to the university college in Clifton.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-Hidden_campus-18) In 1893 [Bristol Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Medical_School "Bristol Medical School") (founded 1833) merged with the university college.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-BristolUniversityHistory-9) However, women were forbidden to take examinations in medicine until 1906.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-archives-hub-19)

The engineering department of the [Merchant Venturers' Technical College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merchant_Venturers'_Technical_College "Merchant Venturers' Technical College") (founded as Bristol Trade and Mining School in 1856) became the engineering faculty of Bristol University in 1909 following disputes with the university college in the 1890s, being finally merged in to the university in 1949.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-Merchant_Venturers-20)

The university college was able to apply for a [royal charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal charter") due to the financial support of the [Wills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._D._&_H._O._Wills "W. D. & H. O. Wills") and [Fry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Fry "Lewis Fry") families, who made their fortunes in tobacco plantations and chocolate respectively (while there was no funding to the university college from [Edward Colston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Colston "Edward Colston"), the trade school that became the Merchant Venturers' Technical College and then the university's engineering faculty was run by the Colston Trustees until 1885).[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-Merchant_Venturers-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-21) A 2018 study commissioned by the university estimated 85% of the philanthropic funds used for the institution's foundation "depended on the labour of enslaved people".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-22)

### Early years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Bristol&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early years")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/University_of_bristol_tower_after_cleaning_arp.jpg/250px-University_of_bristol_tower_after_cleaning_arp.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_bristol_tower_after_cleaning_arp.jpg)

[Wills Memorial Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wills_Memorial_Building "Wills Memorial Building") (Schools of Law and Earth Sciences) on [Park Street, Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Street,_Bristol "Park Street, Bristol"). The tower was cleaned in 2006–2007.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-23)

In 1908, gifts from the Fry and Wills families, particularly £100,000 from [Henry Overton Wills III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Overton_Wills_III "Henry Overton Wills III") (£6m in today's money), were provided to endow a university for Bristol and the West of England, provided that a [royal charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal charter") could be obtained within two years. In December 1909, the king granted the charter.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-charter-24) Henry Wills became its first [chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_(education) "Chancellor (education)") and [Conwy Lloyd Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conwy_Lloyd_Morgan "Conwy Lloyd Morgan") the first vice-chancellor.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-past-officers-25) Wills died in 1911 and in tribute his sons [George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Alfred_Wills "George Alfred Wills") and [Harry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Herbert_Wills "Henry Herbert Wills") built the [Wills Memorial Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wills_Memorial_Building "Wills Memorial Building"), started in 1913 and completed in 1925.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-26)

In 1920, George Wills bought the [Victoria Rooms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Rooms_(Bristol) "Victoria Rooms (Bristol)") and endowed them to the university as a [students' union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Students'_union "Students' union").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-BristolUniversityHistory-9)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/King%27s_College_London_Students_Evacuated_To_Bristol%2C_England%2C_1940_D433.jpg/250px-King%27s_College_London_Students_Evacuated_To_Bristol%2C_England%2C_1940_D433.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King's_College_London_Students_Evacuated_To_Bristol,_England,_1940_D433.jpg)

Evacuated [King's College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_College_London "King's College London") students at the University of Bristol in 1940

[Paul Dirac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Dirac "Paul Dirac") graduated from Bristol in 1921 with a degree in engineering, before obtaining a second degree in mathematics in 1923 from Cambridge. For his subsequent pioneering work on quantum mechanics, he was awarded the 1933 [Nobel Prize in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-27) Later in the 1920s, the H. H. Wills Physics Laboratory was opened by [Ernest Rutherford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Rutherford "Ernest Rutherford").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-28)

The students' union was formed in October 1924 by the merger of the university guild and the university club.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-SU100-29)

[Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill") became the university's third chancellor in 1929, serving the university in that capacity until 1965. He succeeded [Richard Haldane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Haldane "Richard Haldane"), who had held the office from 1912 following the death of Henry Wills.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-archives-hub-19)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-past-officers-25)

During World War II, the Wills Memorial was bombed in the [Bristol Blitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Blitz "Bristol Blitz"), destroying the great hall and its organ along with thousands of books from the library of [King's College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_College_London "King's College London") that had been moved to Bristol for safe keeping. The great hall did not reopen until 1963.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-30)

### Post-war development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Bristol&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Post-war development")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Victoria_Rooms_%28750px%29.jpg/250px-Victoria_Rooms_%28750px%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Victoria_Rooms_(750px).jpg)

The Victoria Rooms, housing the School of Music

In 1947, the university established the first degree in drama in the country.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-31)[_[independent source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Independent\_sources "Wikipedia:Independent sources")_] In the same year, Bristol began offering special entrance [exams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exam "Exam") and [grants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_(money) "Grant (money)") to aid the resettlement of servicemen returning home.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1965, the students' union moved to the Richmond Building.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-SU100-29)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-Hidden_campus-18) This has been noted as an example of the trend to students' union buildings "of vast proportions" in the 1960s and 1970s.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-32)

In 1968, Bristol students held a sit-in as part of a national campaign for students to have more representation on university governing bodies and for widening access. In Bristol they also called for students from other establishments in the city to be allowed to join the union.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-SU100-29)

A series of chancellors and vice-chancellors led the university through these decades, with [Henry Somerset, 10th Duke of Beaufort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Somerset,_10th_Duke_of_Beaufort "Henry Somerset, 10th Duke of Beaufort") taking over from Churchill as chancellor in 1965 before being succeeded by [Dorothy Hodgkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Hodgkin "Dorothy Hodgkin") in 1970 who spent the next 18 years in the office.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-past-officers-25)

One of the few [centres for deaf studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Deaf_Studies,_Bristol "Centre for Deaf Studies, Bristol") in the United Kingdom was established in Bristol in 1981, followed in 1988 by the Norah Fry Centre for research into learning difficulties.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1989, Sir [Jeremy Morse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Morse "Jeremy Morse"), then chairman of [Lloyds Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyds_Bank "Lloyds Bank"), became chancellor.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-past-officers-25)

### 21st century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Bristol&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 21st century")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/University_of_Bristol%2C_School_of_Chemistry.jpg/250px-University_of_Bristol%2C_School_of_Chemistry.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Bristol,_School_of_Chemistry.jpg)

School of Chemistry in 2003

Growth in the number of postgraduate students lead to the establishment of the postgraduate union in 2000.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-33)

In 2002, the university was involved in an argument over press intrusion after details of then-prime minister [Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair")'s son's application to university were published in national newspapers. In the same year, the university opened the new Centre for Sports, Exercise and Health in the university precinct.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-34) At a cost, local residents can also use the facilities.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-35)

[Brenda Hale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brenda_Hale,_Baroness_Hale_of_Richmond "Brenda Hale, Baroness Hale of Richmond"), the first female [Law Lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_Lord "Law Lord"), became chancellor of the university in 2003.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-archives-hub-19)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-past-officers-25)[Paul Nurse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Nurse "Paul Nurse") succeeded Lady Hale as chancellor on 1 January 2017.

In 2004, the Faculty of Engineering completed work on the Bristol Laboratory for Advanced Dynamics Engineering (BLADE), [[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-37) It was built as an extension to the Queen's Building and was officially opened by [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_II "Queen Elizabeth II") in March 2005.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In January 2005, the School of Chemistry was awarded £4.5m by the [Higher Education Funding Council for England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_Education_Funding_Council_for_England "Higher Education Funding Council for England") to create Bristol ChemLabS: a Centre for Excellence in Teaching & Learning (CETL),[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-38) with an additional £350k announced for the capital part of the project in February 2006. Bristol ChemLabS stands for Bristol Chemical Laboratory Sciences; it is the only chemistry CETL in the UK.

September 2009 saw the opening of the university's [Centre for Nanoscience and Quantum Information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Nanoscience_and_Quantum_Information "Centre for Nanoscience and Quantum Information").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-39)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Bristol_University_from_Cabot_Tower.jpg/250px-Bristol_University_from_Cabot_Tower.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bristol_University_from_Cabot_Tower.jpg)

Most of the buildings here are used by the university. The [Wills Memorial Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wills_Memorial_Building "Wills Memorial Building") is left of centre. Viewed from the [Cabot Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabot_Tower_(Bristol) "Cabot Tower (Bristol)") on Brandon Hill

Redevelopment of the centre of the university precinct began in September 2011, with the start of construction of a new life sciences building.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-40)

In 2018 while building work was underway in the [Fry Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fry_Building "Fry Building"),[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-42) the building caught fire.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-44)

In 2022, a judge found that the University of Bristol had contributed to a student's death by failing to make reasonable accommodations.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-45)

In October 2021, Bristol dismissed Professor [David Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Miller_(sociologist) "David Miller (sociologist)") following accusations of [antisemitism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism "Antisemitism") and an internal investigation.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-48) An employment tribunal found in February 2024 that his anti-Zionist beliefs were protected under equality law.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-49) The University of Bristol unsuccessfully appealed the ruling at the [Employment Appeal Tribunal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Employment_Appeal_Tribunal "Employment Appeal Tribunal") in February 2025.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-b247-20260805-50)

In 2024 the university revised their emblem, removing the dolphin emblem because of its connection to the slave trader Edward Colston and adding an image of moving pages and a bookmark.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-51)

In 2025, BristolSEDS, a student society within the university, successfully hot-fired a 6 kilonewton bi-propellant rocket engine, claiming the record for the highest thrust of an engine of this type designed by students in the UK.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-52)

### Buildings and sites

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Bristol&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Buildings and sites")]

The university does not have a main campus but is spread over a considerable geographic area. Most of its activities, however, are concentrated in the area of the city centre, referred to as the "University Precinct".

Some of the University of Bristol's buildings date to its pre-charter days when it was [University College Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_College_Bristol "University College Bristol"). These buildings were designed by [Charles Hansom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Hansom "Charles Hansom"), and suffered being built in stages due to financial pressure. The first large scale building project the University of Bristol undertook on gaining a charter was the [Wills Memorial Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wills_Memorial_Building "Wills Memorial Building"). Other notable buildings and sites include [Royal Fort House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Fort_House "Royal Fort House"), the [University of Bristol Botanic Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol_Botanic_Garden "University of Bristol Botanic Garden"), many large Victorian houses which were converted for teaching in the Faculty of Arts,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-53) and [the Victoria Rooms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Victoria_Rooms "The Victoria Rooms") which house the Music Department and were designed by [Charles Dyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dyer_(architect) "Charles Dyer (architect)"). The [tympanum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tympanum_(architecture) "Tympanum (architecture)") of the building depicts a scene from _The Advent of Morning_ designed by Jabez Tyley.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-54)

[Goldney gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldney_gardens "Goldney gardens") entered the property of the University of Bristol through [George Wills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Alfred_Wills "George Alfred Wills") who had hoped to build an all-male hall of residence there. This was prevented due to the moral objection of the then warden of Clifton Hill House who objected to the idea of male and female residences being in such close proximity. University records show that Miss Starvey was prepared to resign over the issue and that she had the support of the then Chancellor [Conwy Lloyd Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conwy_Lloyd_Morgan "Conwy Lloyd Morgan").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-55) Eventually land was purchased in [Stoke Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoke_Bishop "Stoke Bishop"), allowing the building of what has been described as a "quasi-[Oxbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxbridge "Oxbridge")" hall, [Wills Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wills_Hall "Wills Hall"), to which was added the Dame Monica Wills Chapel by George Wills' widow after his death. When Goldney did become student accommodation in 1956, the flats were designed by Michael Grice who received an award from the Civic Trust for their design.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-56)

Many of the more modern buildings, including Senate House and the newer parts of the HH Wills Physics Laboratory, were designed by Ralph Brentnall using funds from the University Grants Committee. He is also responsible for the extension to the Wills Memorial Building library which was completed to such standard that few now realise that is an extension to the original building.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-57)

In May 2022, the university announced the opening of the Gambling Harms and Research Centre (GHRC). The centre worth £4 million aims to increase awareness and understanding of the dangers of gambling. The project was funded by the GambleAware charity, which chose the university for its history in researching gambling issues, and will integrate research from six facilities.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-58)

### Planned expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Bristol&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Planned expansion")]

In November 2016, the university announced that it plans to build a £300 million Temple Quarter Campus for c. 5,000 students, next to [Bristol Temple Meads railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Temple_Meads_railway_station "Bristol Temple Meads railway station") within [Bristol Temple Quarter Enterprise Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Temple_Quarter_Enterprise_Zone "Bristol Temple Quarter Enterprise Zone"). The new campus, which will include a [business school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_school "Business school"), digital research facilities and a student village, is expected to open in 2021.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-59) For the existing campus, there are plans to remodel Tyndall Avenue, pedestrianise the surrounding area and build a new library and resource hub.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-60)

## Organisation and governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Bristol&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Organisation and governance")]

Main article: [Governance of the University of Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governance_of_the_University_of_Bristol "Governance of the University of Bristol")

In common with most UK universities, Bristol is headed formally by the [chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_(education) "Chancellor (education)"), currently [Sir Paul Nurse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Paul_Nurse "Sir Paul Nurse") and led on a day-to-day basis by the [vice-chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice-chancellor "Vice-chancellor"), currently Professor Evelyn Welch, who is the academic leader and chief executive. There are four pro vice-chancellors and three ceremonial pro-chancellors.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-gov-61) The chancellor may hold office for up to ten years and the pro-chancellors for up to three, unless the University Court determines otherwise,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-63) but the vice-chancellor and pro-vice-chancellors have no term limits.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-65) The vice-chancellor is supported by a deputy vice-chancellor.

Responsibility for running the university is held at an executive level by the vice-chancellor, but the council is the only body that can recommend changes to the university's statutes and charter,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-council-66) with the exception of academic ordinances. These can only be made with the consent of the senate, the chief academic body in the university which also holds responsibility for teaching and learning, examinations and research and enterprise.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-council-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-67) The chancellor and pro chancellors are nominated by council and appointed formally by court, whose additional powers are now limited to these appointments and a few others, including some lay members of council.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-68) Finally, Convocation, the body of all staff, ceremonial officers and graduates of the university, returns 100 members to court and one member to council,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-gov-61) but is otherwise principally a forum for discussion and to ensure graduates stay in touch with the university.

The university is made up of a number of schools and departments organised into three faculties:[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-69)

The university specifies a mix of Cambridge and Oxford [academic dress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_dress "Academic dress"). For the most part, it uses Oxford-style gowns and Cambridge-style hoods, which are required to be 'university red'[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-costume-70) (see the logo at the top of the page).

### Degrees

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Bristol&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Degrees")]

Bristol awards a range of [academic degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_degree "Academic degree") spanning bachelor's and master's degrees as well as junior doctorates and [higher doctorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_doctorate "Higher doctorate"). The [postnominals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postnominals "Postnominals") awarded are the [degree abbreviations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_degree_abbreviations "British degree abbreviations") used commonly among British universities. The university is part of the [Engineering Doctorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering_Doctorate "Engineering Doctorate") scheme,[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-71) and awards the Eng. D. in [systems engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_engineering "Systems engineering"), [engineering management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering_management "Engineering management"), [aerospace engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_engineering "Aerospace engineering") and [non-destructive evaluation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-destructive_evaluation "Non-destructive evaluation").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-72)

Bristol notably does not award by title any bachelor's degrees in music, which is available for study but awarded BA (although it does award MMus and DMus), nor any degree in [divinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divinity "Divinity"), since divinity is not available for study (students of theology are awarded a BA). Similarly, the university does not award BLitt (Bachelor of Letters), although it does award both MLitt and [DLitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DLitt "DLitt"). In regulations, the university does not name MD or [DDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Dental_Surgery "Doctor of Dental Surgery") as [higher doctorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_doctorate "Higher doctorate"), although they are in many universities[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-73) as these degrees are normally accredited professional doctorates.

The degrees of DLitt, DSc, DEng, [LLD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Laws "Doctor of Laws") and DMus, whilst having regulations specifying the grounds for award,[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-74) are most often conferred as honorary degrees (_in honoris causa_).[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-75) Those used most commonly are the DLitt, DSc and LLD, with the [MA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Arts "Master of Arts") (and occasionally the MLitt) also sometimes conferred honorarily for distinction in the local area or within the university.

### Finances

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Bristol&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Finances")]

In the financial year ending 31 July 2024, Bristol had a total income of £1.060 billion (2022/23 – £902.2 million) and total expenditure of £768.7 million (2022/23 – £807.5 million).[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-Bristol_Financial_Statement_23/24-76) Key sources of income included £459.9 million from tuition fees and education contracts (2022/23 – £416.4 million), £119 million from funding body grants (2022/23 – £127.7 million), £294.1 million from research grants and contracts (2022/23 – £203.3 million), £16.5 million from investment income (2022/23 – £13.6 million) and £8.9 million from endowment donations (2022/23 – £0.6 million).[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-Bristol_Financial_Statement_23/24-76)

At year end, Bristol had endowments of £98.7 million (2023 – £86.1 million) and total net assets of £1.581 billion (2023 – £1.256 billion). It holds the [fifteenth-largest endowment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_UK_universities_by_endowment "List of UK universities by endowment") of any university in the UK.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-Bristol_Financial_Statement_23/24-76)

### Logo and arms

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Bristol&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Logo and arms")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/University_of_Bristol_Arms.svg/250px-University_of_Bristol_Arms.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Bristol_Arms.svg)

Coat of Arms

In 2004, the university unveiled its new logo. The icons in the logo are the sun for the Wills family, the dolphin for Colston, the horse for Fry and the ship-and-castle from the medieval seal of the City of Bristol, as also used in the coat of arms. The shape of the whole logo represents the open book of learning.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-vis-ident-7) This logo has replaced the university [arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms "Coat of arms") shown, but the arms continue to be used where there is a specific historical or ceremonial requirement. The arms comprise:

_argent on a cross quadrate gules the arms of the City of Bristol between in pale and a sun in splendour (for Wills) and an open book proper, leaved and clasped or, and inscribed with the words Nisi quia Dominus, and in fesse to the sinister a dolphin embowed (for Colston), and to the dexter a horse courant (for Fry), both of the third._

The inscription on the book is the [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin") opening of the 124th Psalm, _"If the Lord Himself had not (been on our side...)"_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-arms-1) The Latin motto granted with the Arms below the shields is Vim promovet insitam, from the fourth Ode of Horace's fourth book meaning '[Learning] promotes one's innate power'.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-77)

## Publishing and commercial activities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Bristol&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Publishing and commercial activities")]

### Bristol University Press

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Bristol&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Bristol University Press")]

Bristol University Press is a scholarly press based at the University of Bristol.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-brupr-121) In 1996, [Alison Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alison_Shaw_(publisher)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alison Shaw (publisher) (page does not exist)") founded **Policy Press** at the University of Bristol, as an [academic publisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_publisher "Academic publisher") based in the Faculty of Social Sciences and Law and specialising in the social sciences. In October 2016, Policy Press became an imprint of the newly founded **Bristol University Press**.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-122)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-123)

It is not-for-profit university press which publishes 22 journals and 200 books a year in subjects including: Ageing and Gerontology, Business and Management, Criminology, Economics and Society, Environment and Sustainability, International Development, Law, Politics and International Relations, Science, Technology and Society, and Sociology. It achieved journal citation metrics with gains in Journal Impact Factors and improved results in Journal Citation Indicator, Scopus CiteScore and SJR.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-buppr-124)

### Bristol is Open

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Bristol&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Bristol is Open")]

Bristol is Open, abbreviated as BiO, is a joint venture project between [Bristol City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_City_Council "Bristol City Council") and University of Bristol. It is for delivering research contributing to the development of a Smart City and deploying a city-scale open and programmable testbed for experimentation and digital innovation.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-biojv-125) The collaboration of two organisations started in April 2015 and ended in December 2019 with Bristol City Council taking full control of BiO's operations.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bristol#cite_note-biopn-126) It has completed many technical trials and experiments including open access to Wi-Fi as a reduction of the digital divide and development for Smart City technology.

## Student life
